the-deluge.s: The Deluge refers to the Swedish invasion and occupation of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth between 1655 and 1660, alongside wider wars with Russia and others. The devastation of towns, population and economy was severe, and the episode is regarded as a turning point in the…

the-gambia.s: The Gambia is a small country in West Africa along the Gambia River. The region formed part of the sphere of the Kaabu Empire, a Mandinka state that dominated the Senegambia region for several centuries.

the-great-game.s: The Great Game was the nineteenth-century rivalry between the British and Russian Empires for influence in Central Asia, Afghanistan and Persia. Russian expansion towards Afghanistan brought the two empires close, and the Sikh Empire served as a buffer between British India…

table-of-ranks.s: The Table of Ranks was a system of formal grades for military, civil and court service introduced by Peter the Great in 1722. It linked status to state service and allowed men of non-noble birth to acquire noble rank by advancing through its grades.

tabriz.s: Tabriz is a city in north-western Iran, historically one of the principal commercial and political centres of the region. Under the Ilkhanate it became a major hub of trade where Mongol, Persian, Armenian and European merchants met.

tacitus.s: Tacitus was a Roman historian and senator of the late first and early second centuries CE, author of the Annals, the Histories and other works. His writings are a major source for the early Roman Empire and its frontiers.

tadeusz-kosciuszko.s: Tadeusz Kościuszko was a Polish-Lithuanian military engineer and commander who also served in the American War of Independence. In 1794 he led a national insurrection against Russian and Prussian domination of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

taghaza.s: Taghaza was a salt-mining centre in the western Sahara, in the north of present-day Mali. Its rock-salt deposits were among the most important sources of salt for West Africa, exchanged southwards for gold.

tagus.s: The Tagus is the longest river of the Iberian Peninsula, flowing westwards through central Spain past Toledo and reaching the Atlantic at Lisbon. In the medieval period it formed an approximate frontier zone between Christian kingdoms and Muslim al-Andalus.

taharqa.s: Taharqa was a king of Kush and pharaoh of Egypt of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the seventh century BCE, one of the most powerful Kushite rulers. He undertook major building works in Egypt and Nubia and resisted Assyrian expansion into Egypt.

tahirid-dynasty.s: The Tahirid dynasty was a line of governors who ruled Khurasan in the ninth century, founded by Tahir ibn Husayn, a general of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun. Although they acknowledged Abbasid authority, the Tahirids governed with considerable hereditary autonomy.

tahmasp-ii.s: Tahmasp II was a Safavid prince who claimed the throne of Iran after the Afghan capture of Isfahan in 1722 brought down his father's rule. The warlord Nader, then known as Nader Qoli, rose to prominence in his service and expelled Afghan, Ottoman and Russian occupiers in his…

taifa.s: Taifa refers to the independent Muslim kingdoms into which al-Andalus fragmented after the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba in the early eleventh century. Weak and often at war with one another, the taifa kings paid tribute to Christian rulers.

taiho-code.s: The Taihō Code was a Japanese legal and administrative code promulgated in 701. Modelled on the penal and administrative statutes of Tang China, it established a centralised bureaucratic state under the emperor.

taika-reform.s: The Taika Reform was a programme of political reforms begun in Japan in 645. Inspired by Chinese models, it sought to strengthen the imperial court, bring land and people under state control and create a centralised administration.

taiping-rebellion.s: The Taiping Rebellion was a massive civil war in China between 1850 and 1864, led by Hong Xiuquan, who proclaimed a Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace inspired by his own version of Christianity. One of the deadliest conflicts in history, it caused tens of millions of deaths and…

taisho-period.s: The Taishō period was the era of Japanese history corresponding to the reign of Emperor Taishō, from 1912 to 1926. It is associated with a growth of party politics, parliamentary government and liberal ideas, often called Taishō democracy.

taiwan.s: Taiwan is a large island off the south-eastern coast of China. The Dutch established a colony there in the seventeenth century but lost it to Koxinga's forces in 1662, and the Qing took the island from the Zheng family in 1683.

taj-mahal.s: The Taj Mahal is a white marble mausoleum in Agra, northern India, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the seventeenth century in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Combining Persian, Central Asian and Indian architectural traditions, it is widely regarded as the…

talent.s: The talent was a large unit of weight used in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East, commonly used to measure quantities of silver and gold for payments. Indemnities imposed by victorious powers were often reckoned in talents.

talmudic-academy.s: A Talmudic academy, or yeshiva, is an institution for the advanced study of the Talmud and Jewish law. Such academies flourished in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, whose cities became the heartland of Ashkenazi Jewish civilisation.

tang-campaign-against-the-eastern-turks.n: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks
tang-campaign-against-the-eastern-turks.s: The Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks was a military expedition launched by Emperor Taizong that defeated the Eastern Turkic Khaganate in 630 CE. The capture of its ruler brought the steppe peoples north of China under Tang overlordship, and Taizong accepted the title of…

tang-code.s: The Tang Code was the comprehensive penal code of the Tang Dynasty, issued with an official commentary, the Tang Lü Shuyi, in 653. It defined crimes and punishments systematically and reflected Confucian principles of hierarchy and family relationships.

tang-dynasty.s: The Tang Dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907 and is often regarded as a high point of Chinese civilisation. Its capital Chang'an was a cosmopolitan centre linked to Central Asia by the Silk Road, and its institutions, law and culture influenced Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

tanis.s: Tanis was an ancient city in the north-eastern Nile Delta of Egypt. At the end of the New Kingdom it became the seat of Smendes, who controlled Lower Egypt while the High Priests of Amun governed Upper Egypt from Thebes.

tanka.s: The tanka was a silver coin introduced as standard currency in the Delhi Sultanate by Iltutmish in the early thirteenth century. It became the basis of the sultanate's monetary system and was later echoed in the rupee of subsequent Indian states.

tanzimat.s: The Tanzimat was a period of reform in the Ottoman Empire from 1839 to 1876. Prompted by growing European military and economic superiority, it sought to modernise administration, law, taxation and the army, and proclaimed the equality of Ottoman subjects regardless of religion.

taoism.s: Taoism, or Daoism, is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centred on the Dao, or Way, and associated with texts such as the Daodejing. In the early Han Dynasty, Taoist-influenced ideas of minimal government shaped imperial policy.

targowica-confederation.s: The Targowica Confederation was an alliance of Polish-Lithuanian magnates formed in 1792 to overturn the reformist Constitution of 3 May 1791. Backed by Catherine the Great, it invited Russian military intervention.

tarhunt.s: Tarhunt, also called Tarhun, was the storm god of the Hittites and other Anatolian peoples and one of the chief deities of the Hittite pantheon. The Hittite Empire profile explains that the Hittite king ruled as the earthly representative of the storm god rather than as a god…

tarim-basin.s: The Tarim Basin is a large desert basin in Central Asia, in present-day Xinjiang, ringed by oasis cities that served as key stations on the Silk Road. Control of these oases was repeatedly contested by Chinese, steppe and Central Asian powers.

tariq-ibn-ziyad.s: Tariq ibn Ziyad was a Berber commander in the service of the Umayyad Caliphate who led the Muslim invasion of the Iberian Peninsula in 711 CE. After crossing from North Africa he defeated the Visigothic king Roderic, opening the way to the conquest of most of Iberia.

tarmashirin.s: Tarmashirin was a khan of the Chagatai Empire who died in 1334. He converted to Islam, moved the khanate's administrative centre towards the cities of Transoxiana and led a raid deep into the Delhi Sultanate around 1329.

tatars.s: Tatars is a name applied to various Turkic-speaking peoples of the Eurasian steppe, including the Crimean Tatars who raided and fought along the borders of eastern Europe. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth both fought against Tatar raiders and drew on Tatar and Cossack…

taurus-mountains.s: The Taurus Mountains are a mountain range in southern Anatolia, separating the Anatolian plateau from the Mediterranean coast and northern Syria. They formed a natural barrier and frontier in many periods of history.

tawhid.s: Tawhid is the Islamic doctrine of the absolute oneness and unity of God, a central principle of Islamic theology. The reformer Ibn Tumart placed an uncompromising interpretation of tawhid at the heart of his teaching.

taxila.s: Taxila was an ancient city in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, in present-day Pakistan, renowned as a centre of trade and learning. It lay on routes connecting India with Central Asia and Iran.

tayma.s: Tayma is an oasis town in north-western Arabia that was an important stop on ancient caravan routes. The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus resided there for around a decade in the sixth century BCE, leaving Babylon in the hands of his son.

tea.s: Tea is a beverage made from the leaves of the tea plant, native to southern China. Under the Song Dynasty tea became a major commodity and source of state revenue, and in Japan tea culture flourished under the Tokugawa Shogunate.

technical-university.s: A technical university is a higher education institution specialising in engineering, applied sciences and technology. In nineteenth-century Germany a dense network of such institutions trained engineers and chemists for industry.

teispes.s: Teispes was an early Persian ruler of the seventh century BCE and an ancestor of Cyrus the Great in the Achaemenid line. The Elamite Confederation profile notes that he had conquered Anshan, a key Elamite region, around 650 BCE.

telegraph.s: The telegraph was a system for transmitting messages over long distances by electrical signals along wires, developed in the nineteenth century. Submarine cables linked Britain with India, Australia and other parts of its empire, greatly accelerating imperial communication and…

tell-leilan.s: Tell Leilan is an archaeological site in north-eastern Syria, the remains of an ancient city of upper Mesopotamia. Excavations suggest that it was abandoned around the late third millennium BCE.

temasek.s: Temasek is an early name for the settlement on the island of Singapore at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. By the fourteenth century it had become a trading port in the region once dominated by Srivijaya.

temple-in-jerusalem.s: The Temple in Jerusalem was the central sanctuary of ancient Jewish worship. After the first temple was destroyed by the Babylonians, the Achaemenid king Cyrus the Great permitted exiled Jews to return and rebuild it, and the Second Temple was completed in the late sixth…

templo-mayor.s: The Templo Mayor was the great twin-temple pyramid at the centre of Tenochtitlan, dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. It was enlarged in successive building phases, and its expanded form was rededicated in 1487 under the ruler Ahuitzotl.

ten-great-campaigns.s: The Ten Great Campaigns were a series of military campaigns conducted under the Qianlong Emperor between 1755 and 1792. They included wars against the Dzungars, campaigns in Xinjiang, Sichuan, Taiwan, Burma and Vietnam, and expeditions against the Gurkhas of Nepal.

ten-lost-tribes.s: The Ten Lost Tribes are the tribes of the northern Kingdom of Israel that, according to biblical tradition, disappeared from history after the Assyrian conquest of Israel and the deportation of its population in 722 BCE. The Assyrian Empire profile notes that this experience…

tenancy.s: Tenancy is an arrangement in which cultivators farm land owned by others in return for rent, labour or a share of the harvest. In the later Han Dynasty, large landowners absorbed peasant smallholders into dependent tenancy, removing them from the tax registers.

tenochtitlan.s: Tenochtitlan was the capital city of the Mexica and of the Aztec Empire, founded in the fourteenth century on an island in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico. Connected to the shore by causeways and supported by chinampa agriculture, it grew into one of the largest cities in…

tenryo.s: Tenryō was the term for the lands directly administered by the Tokugawa Shogunate in Edo-period Japan. The Tokugawa Shogunate profile states that these territories covered approximately 25 percent of Japan's productive land, including major cities and mines.

tepanec-war.s: The Tepanec War was the conflict of 1428 in which the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan, overthrew the dominant Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco. It followed the death of the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc and the succession struggle that ensued under his son Maxtla.

tepanecs.s: The Tepanecs were a Nahua people of the Valley of Mexico whose state, centred on Azcapotzalco, dominated the region in the early fifteenth century. The Mexica of Tenochtitlan initially served them as tributaries and mercenary warriors.

tequihua.s: Tequihua was a prestigious rank in the Aztec military hierarchy awarded to warriors who had captured a set number of enemies in battle. The Aztec Empire profile states that a warrior who captured four enemies achieved this rank, gaining access to the elite Eagle and Jaguar…

tercio.s: The tercio was a Spanish infantry formation of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries that combined pikemen, swordsmen and arquebusiers in large, disciplined squares. It made the armies of the Spanish Empire among the most formidable in Europe.

terror-as-policy.s: Terror as policy refers to the deliberate use of massacre, mass deportation, mutilation and spectacular atrocity by states to deter resistance and compel submission. Such tactics could reduce the cost of conquest by persuading cities to surrender, but often bred lasting…

tetrarchy.s: The Tetrarchy was the system of imperial government established by Diocletian in 293 CE, under which the Roman Empire was ruled by four emperors: two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars. Each was responsible for a different region, allowing closer defence of the frontiers.

tewodros-ii.s: Tewodros II was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1855 until his death in 1868. Rising from a provincial background, he ended the era of regional fragmentation known as the Zemene Mesafint and sought to centralise and modernise the state.

texcoco.s: Texcoco was a major city-state on the eastern shore of Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico and one of the three members of the Aztec Triple Alliance. Renowned as a centre of law, poetry and learning, especially under its ruler Nezahualcoyotl, it received two-fifths of the…

tezozomoc.s: Tezozomoc was the long-reigning ruler of the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco, which dominated the Valley of Mexico in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. He died in 1426.

thailand.s: Thailand is a country in mainland Southeast Asia, historically home to a succession of kingdoms including Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. The Gupta Empire profile notes that Gupta religious art and iconography shaped artistic traditions in Thailand, Cambodia and Java.

thalassocracy.s: A thalassocracy is a state whose power rests primarily on control of the sea, maritime trade routes and ports rather than on large land territories. The Srivijaya Empire is a classic example, dominating the straits of Southeast Asia from the seventh to the thirteenth centuries.

theatre.s: Theatre is the performance of drama before an audience, and also the buildings designed for it. The Seleucid Empire spread Greek urban forms, including the theatre, into regions of the Near East and Iran that had no previous tradition of such civic institutions.

thebes.s: Thebes was an ancient city in Upper Egypt on the Nile, the site of present-day Luxor. It was the religious centre of the god Amun, with the great temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor, and the nearby Valley of the Kings held New Kingdom royal tombs.

theme-system.s: The theme system was the military and administrative organisation of the Byzantine Empire from around the seventh century, in which provinces called themes were governed by military commanders. Soldiers were supported by grants of land in return for hereditary military service.

theodor-herzl.s: Theodor Herzl was a Jewish journalist and writer born in Budapest and active in Vienna, regarded as the founder of modern political Zionism. In works such as The Jewish State (1896) he called for a Jewish national homeland, and he convened the first Zionist Congress in 1897.

theodosius-i.s: Theodosius I was a Roman emperor who died in 395 CE, the last to rule both the eastern and western halves of the empire. He made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the state.

theodulf-of-orleans.s: Theodulf of Orléans was a scholar, poet and bishop at the court of Charlemagne, of Visigothic origin. He was one of the leading figures of the Carolingian Renaissance, promoting education and the correction of religious texts.

theravada-buddhism.s: Theravada Buddhism is the branch of Buddhism that relies on the Pali canon and became dominant in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia. Its spread in the later period of the Khmer Empire emphasised monastic communities and individual merit.

third-anglo-ashanti-war.s: The Third Anglo-Ashanti War was a conflict between the British Empire and the Ashanti Empire, culminating in 1874. A British expedition under Garnet Wolseley reached and burned the Ashanti capital Kumasi.

third-battle-of-panipat.s: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought in 1761 near Panipat in northern India between the Maratha Empire and the invading army of the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani and his allies. It was one of the largest battles of the eighteenth century and ended in a crushing Maratha…

third-crusade.s: The Third Crusade was a military expedition by European Christian powers from 1189 to 1192, launched after Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187. Led by Richard I of England, Philip II of France and, until his death on the way, Frederick Barbarossa, it recovered Acre and much…

third-dynasty-of-ur.s: The Third Dynasty of Ur, also called Ur III or the Neo-Sumerian Empire, was a Mesopotamian state that ruled from the city of Ur from 2112 to 2004 BCE. Founded by Ur-Nammu, it built a highly centralised bureaucratic administration on Akkadian precedents.

third-partition-of-poland.s: The Third Partition of Poland was the final division of the remaining territory of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth among Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1795. It followed the defeat of Tadeusz Kościuszko's insurrection of 1794.

third-punic-war.s: The Third Punic War was the last conflict between Rome and Carthage, fought from 149 to 146 BCE. After a long siege, Roman forces captured and destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE, and its territory became the Roman province of Africa.

thirty-years-war.s: The Thirty Years' War was a series of conflicts fought mainly in central Europe from 1618 to 1648, beginning as a religious struggle within the Holy Roman Empire and widening into a contest among the major European powers. It devastated large parts of Germany.

thirty-five-years-in-the-east.s: Thirty-five Years in the East is a memoir by Johann Martin Honigberger, a European physician who served at the court of the Sikh Empire in Lahore. It describes his travels and experiences in the Punjab and neighbouring regions.

thomas-aquinas.s: Thomas Aquinas was a thirteenth-century Italian Dominican friar and theologian, the most influential philosopher of medieval scholasticism. His synthesis of Christian theology and Aristotelian philosophy drew on Latin translations of Aristotle and of commentaries by Muslim…

thomas-bowdich.s: Thomas Bowdich was an English traveller and writer who visited Kumasi, the Ashanti capital, as a British envoy in 1817. His published account is a major early European source on the Ashanti Empire.

three-departments-and-six-ministries.s: The Three Departments and Six Ministries was the central administrative structure of the Tang Dynasty. The three departments drafted, reviewed and implemented policy, while the six ministries handled personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice and public works.

three-kingdoms-period.s: The Three Kingdoms period was the era of Chinese history following the collapse of the Han Dynasty, during which the states of Wei, Shu and Wu contended for supremacy in the third century CE. It was marked by prolonged warfare and became one of the most celebrated periods in…

thutmose-i.s: Thutmose I was a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the early New Kingdom. He led military campaigns deep into Nubia and as far as the Euphrates in Syria, greatly extending Egyptian power.

thutmose-iii.s: Thutmose III was a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt and one of the most successful military rulers in its history. After the co-regency with Hatshepsut, he conducted numerous campaigns in the Levant, including the victory at Megiddo, and consolidated Egyptian control…

thutmose-iv.s: Thutmose IV was a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the fourteenth century BCE. His reign saw the establishment of peaceful relations with the kingdom of Mitanni after earlier rivalry.

tiber-river.s: The Tiber is a river of central Italy that flows through Rome to the Tyrrhenian Sea. Rome grew up at a crossing of the river, with access to the coast and to inland trade routes.

tibet.s: Tibet is a high plateau region of Central Asia, north of the Himalayas, with a distinct language and Buddhist culture. It was brought under Qing overlordship in the eighteenth century.

tibetan-buddhism.s: Tibetan Buddhism is the form of Buddhism that developed in Tibet, combining Mahayana and Vajrayana teachings with distinctive monastic institutions. Under the Yuan Dynasty, Tibetan lamas received extraordinary privileges from Kublai Khan onward.

tichitt-culture.s: The Tichitt culture was a prehistoric culture of stone-built settlements in south-eastern Mauritania, centred on the escarpments of Dhar Tichitt and Dhar Walata. The Ghana Empire profile traces the origins of Ghana, or Wagadou, to this culture, which it dates archaeologically…

tiglath-pileser-iii.s: Tiglath-pileser III was king of Assyria from 745 to 727 BCE and the architect of the Neo-Assyrian imperial system. He reorganised provincial administration into smaller units under royal governors, created a standing army, and greatly expanded the use of mass deportation.

tigranes-the-great.s: Tigranes the Great, or Tigranes II, was king of Armenia in the first century BCE, who briefly made Armenia the leading power of the Near East. The Seleucid Empire profile notes that he absorbed the diminished remnant of the Seleucid kingdom between 83 and 69 BCE.

tigris.s: The Tigris is one of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, flowing from eastern Anatolia south-east through Iraq to join the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf. Its waters supported irrigation agriculture and the cities of Assur, Nineveh, Ctesiphon, Seleucia and Baghdad.

timar.s: The timar was a grant of revenue from land in the Ottoman Empire given to a cavalryman, or sipahi, in return for military service. The timar holder collected taxes from the peasants of his assigned territory and served in campaigns with his retainers.

timber.s: Timber is wood used for construction, shipbuilding and fuel, and was a strategic resource for many pre-modern states. The river plains of Mesopotamia lacked good timber, so the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian states imported it from the mountains and the Levant.

timbuktu.s: Timbuktu is a city near the Niger River in present-day Mali, at the southern edge of the Sahara. It became a major centre of the trans-Saharan trade and of Islamic learning under the Mali Empire and reached its height under the Songhai Empire, when its mosques and scholars…

timur.s: Timur, also known as Tamerlane, was a Turco-Mongol conqueror who rose to power in Transoxiana in the late fourteenth century and founded the Timurid Empire. His campaigns stretched from Anatolia to India, including the sack of Delhi in 1398, and were marked by extreme brutality.

timurid-empire.s: The Timurid Empire was the state founded by Timur in the late fourteenth century, centred on Transoxiana, Iran and Afghanistan, with capitals at Samarkand and later Herat. After Timur's death it fragmented among his descendants but became famous for its patronage of Persian…

tin.s: Tin is a metal that, when alloyed with copper, produces bronze, making it a strategic commodity of the ancient world. Because tin deposits were rare, it was traded over long distances.

tinmel.s: Tinmel is a village in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco. In the early twelfth century the religious reformer Ibn Tumart established his base there after proclaiming himself the Mahdi, making it the cradle of the Almohad movement.

tirailleurs.s: Tirailleurs were colonial infantry units of the French army recruited from French territories in Africa and Asia, including Senegal, Algeria and Indochina. They fought in French colonial campaigns and in both world wars.

tlacaelel.s: Tlacaelel was a Mexica statesman and adviser to several rulers of Tenochtitlan in the fifteenth century. The Aztec Empire profile describes him as the ideologist who rewrote Mexica history to provide the theological and political foundation of empire.

tlacatecatl.s: The tlacatecatl was one of the highest military offices in the Aztec Empire, a senior commander of the Mexica army. The Aztec Empire profile notes that the empire was governed through regional tribute collectors and through the tlacatecatl and the tlacochcalcatl, who commanded…

tlacochcalcatl.s: The tlacochcalcatl was one of the two supreme military commanders of the Aztec Empire, whose title is associated with the house of darts, or armoury. Together with the tlacatecatl, he led the Mexica army.

tlacopan.s: Tlacopan was a Tepanec city-state on the western shore of Lake Texcoco and the third member of the Aztec Triple Alliance, alongside Tenochtitlan and Texcoco. It joined the alliance after the defeat of Azcapotzalco in 1428.

tlatelolco.s: Tlatelolco was a Mexica city adjacent to Tenochtitlan, founded on the same island in Lake Texcoco and later absorbed into it. It housed the greatest market of the Aztec world.

tlaxcalans.s: The Tlaxcalans were the people of Tlaxcala, a Nahua confederation east of the Valley of Mexico that remained independent of the Aztec Empire. They were long-standing enemies of the Mexica and fought repeated ritual wars with them.

tlemcen.s: Tlemcen is a city in north-western Algeria that was an important commercial and political centre of the central Maghreb. The Almohad Caliphate profile notes that the Zayyanid seizure of Tlemcen around 1236 carved the central Maghreb out of the Almohad domain.

tofangchi.s: Tofangchi were musketeers in the armies of Safavid and later Iranian states. Under Shah Abbas I they were organised as a corps paid directly from the royal treasury and loyal to the Shah rather than to tribal chiefs.

toghon-temur.s: Toghon Temür was the last emperor of the Yuan Dynasty to rule China. His reign was marked by factional conflict, natural disasters and widespread rebellion, including the Red Turban uprisings.

toghrul-iii.s: Toghrul III was the last sultan of the Great Seljuk line, ruling in western Iran and Iraq in the late twelfth century. The Seljuk Empire profile records that he was killed in battle by the Khwarazmian Shah Tekish in 1194.

togo.s: Togo is a country in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea. As Togoland it was a German colony from the 1880s until the First World War, when it was occupied by British and French forces.

token-currency-of-muhammad-bin-tughlaq.n: Token currency of Muhammad bin Tughlaq
token-currency-of-muhammad-bin-tughlaq.s: The token currency of Muhammad bin Tughlaq was an experiment begun in 1329 in which the Delhi Sultanate issued copper or brass coins to be accepted at the value of silver. Because the tokens were easy to imitate, widespread forgery followed and the scheme collapsed.

tokugawa-hidetada.s: Tokugawa Hidetada was the second shogun of the Tokugawa Shogunate, the son and successor of Tokugawa Ieyasu. He succeeded his father as shogun in 1605 while Ieyasu continued to exercise power in retirement.

tokugawa-ieyasu.s: Tokugawa Ieyasu was a Japanese warlord who founded the Tokugawa Shogunate. After his victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, he was appointed shogun by the imperial court in 1603, inaugurating two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule.

tokugawa-shogunate.s: The Tokugawa Shogunate, or Tokugawa Bakufu, was the military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868 under shoguns of the Tokugawa family, with its seat at Edo. It imposed a long peace, regulated the daimyo, restricted foreign contact and presided over economic and urban…

tokugawa-yoshinobu.s: Tokugawa Yoshinobu was the fifteenth and last shogun of the Tokugawa Shogunate. Facing mounting pressure from anti-shogunate domains and the challenges posed by Western powers, he resigned his powers to the emperor in 1867.

toledo.s: Toledo is a city in central Spain on the River Tagus, the former Visigothic capital and later a major city of al-Andalus. Its capture by Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085 was a turning point in the Christian advance in Iberia.

toluid-civil-war.s: The Toluid Civil War was a succession war fought from 1260 to 1264 between Kublai Khan and his younger brother Ariq Böke, both grandsons of Genghis Khan through Tolui. Kublai's victory secured his position as Great Khan.

tomato.s: The tomato is a fruit-bearing plant native to the Americas that spread to Europe and the rest of the world after the Spanish conquests of the sixteenth century. It became a staple of many cuisines.

tome-de-sousa.s: Tomé de Sousa was a Portuguese nobleman who became the first Governor-General of Brazil in 1549. His appointment partly replaced the decentralised hereditary captaincy system, which had produced very uneven results.

tonle-sap.s: The Tonle Sap is a large freshwater lake in Cambodia connected to the Mekong River, which swells greatly during the monsoon season. Its seasonal flooding and rich fisheries supported dense populations and intensive rice agriculture.

tonyukuk.s: Tonyukuk was a statesman and military adviser of the Second Turkic Khaganate, who died in 726. He served several qaghans and is commemorated in an Old Turkic inscription that recounts his role in rebuilding Turkic power.

topchi.s: Topchi were artillerymen in the armies of the Safavid Empire and other states of the Islamic world. Under Shah Abbas I, a corps of topchi was created alongside ghulam cavalry and tofangchi musketeers.

tophet.s: A tophet was an open-air sanctuary found at Carthage and other Phoenician and Punic sites, containing urns with the cremated remains of infants and young animals. The Punic Empire profile notes that these sanctuaries have generated sustained scholarly debate.

toramana.s: Toramana was a ruler of the Hunas, or Alchon Huns, who invaded north-western India around the late fifth and early sixth centuries CE. The Gupta Empire profile notes that by around 500 CE the Hunas under Toramana and then his successor Mihirakula occupied large parts of…

torna-fort.s: Torna Fort is a hill fort in the Sahyadri range of the Western Ghats, near Pune in western India. Its capture by Shivaji in 1646 was one of his first military successes and is often regarded as the beginning of the Maratha state.

total-war.s: Total war is warfare in which states mobilise their entire population, economy and resources, and in which the distinction between combatants and civilians is eroded. The First World War was a defining example.

total-war-and-attrition.s: Total war and attrition describes a recurring pattern in which prolonged, large-scale conflict drains an empire's manpower, finances and social cohesion faster than they can be replenished. Even victorious states could be fatally weakened by such struggles.

totonacs.s: The Totonacs are an indigenous people of the Gulf Coast of Mexico, centred on the region of present-day Veracruz, whose city of Cempoala was subject to Aztec tribute. When the Spanish landed in 1519 the Totonacs allied with them against the Mexica.

toucouleur.s: Toucouleur refers to the Futa Tooro people of the Senegal River valley and to the West African empire founded by the jihad leader Al-Hajj Umar Tall in the mid-nineteenth century. The Sokoto Caliphate profile notes that Umar Tall's Toucouleur conquests of the 1850s and 1860s…

toussaint-louverture.s: Toussaint Louverture was the leading figure of the Haitian Revolution, a formerly enslaved man who became the commander of the revolutionary forces in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. He defeated rival forces and governed the colony before being captured by Napoleon's…

tower-of-belem.s: The Tower of Belém is a fortified tower on the Tagus estuary at Lisbon, built in the early sixteenth century in the Manueline style. It guarded the approach to the city and became a symbol of the Age of Discovery.

tower-of-skulls.s: A tower of skulls was a structure built from the heads of the slain, raised as a deliberate display of terror after the capture of a city. Timur was notorious for constructing such towers during his campaigns.

toyotomi-clan.s: The Toyotomi clan was the family of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who unified Japan in the late sixteenth century. After his death in 1598 his young heir Hideyori was eclipsed by Tokugawa Ieyasu.

toyotomi-hideyoshi.s: Toyotomi Hideyoshi was a Japanese warlord who rose from humble origins to complete the unification of Japan in the late sixteenth century, succeeding Oda Nobunaga. He conducted a nationwide land survey, disarmed the peasantry and launched invasions of Korea in the 1590s.

trajan.s: Trajan was Roman emperor from 98 to 117 CE, under whom the empire reached its greatest territorial extent. He conquered Dacia in two wars and later campaigned against Parthia, annexing Armenia and Mesopotamia for a time.

trajans-dacian-wars.s: Trajan's Dacian Wars were two campaigns fought by the Roman emperor Trajan against the kingdom of Dacia, north of the Danube, in 101–102 CE and 105–106 CE. The second war ended with the death of the Dacian king Decebalus and the annexation of Dacia as a Roman province,…

transfer-of-capital-to-daulatabad.s: The transfer of capital to Daulatabad was an attempt by Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1327 to move the capital of the Delhi Sultanate from Delhi to Daulatabad, formerly Devagiri, in the Deccan. The aim was to govern the newly conquered south more effectively, but the forced…

transfer-of-the-portuguese-court-to-braz.n: Transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil
transfer-of-the-portuguese-court-to-braz.s: The transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil was the relocation of the Portuguese royal family and government to Rio de Janeiro in 1808, as Napoleon's armies invaded Portugal. Rio became the seat of the Portuguese monarchy, and Brazil was raised in status within the realm.

transhumance.s: Transhumance is the seasonal movement of livestock and herders between different pastures, typically between lowland winter grazing and highland summer grazing. It was common in mountainous regions of the ancient Near East.

transoxiana.s: Transoxiana is the historical name for the region of Central Asia between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, roughly corresponding to modern Uzbekistan and neighbouring areas. Its oasis cities, including Samarkand and Bukhara, were centres of trade and learning on the Silk Road.

trans-saharan-trade.s: The trans-Saharan trade was the network of caravan routes across the Sahara Desert linking North Africa and the Mediterranean with West and Central Africa. Gold, slaves, ivory and other goods moved north, while salt, horses, textiles and manufactured goods moved south, along…

trans-siberian-railway.s: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the railway line linking European Russia with the Pacific coast at Vladivostok, the longest in the world. Construction began in 1891, and the line was largely in operation by 1904.

transylvania.s: Transylvania is a historical region in the Carpathian basin, now part of Romania. It was an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, intervening in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during the Deluge.

treaties-between-rome-and-carthage.s: The treaties between Rome and Carthage were a series of agreements, recorded by the Greek historian Polybius, that defined the two powers' spheres of influence and trade. The earliest is traditionally dated to 509 BCE and a later one to 348 BCE.

treaty-of-addis-ababa.s: The Treaty of Addis Ababa was signed in 1896 between Ethiopia and Italy after the Ethiopian victory at the Battle of Adwa. It annulled the disputed Treaty of Wuchale and recognised Ethiopia's full independence.

treaty-of-amritsar-1809.s: The Treaty of Amritsar of 1809 was an agreement between Ranjit Singh and the British East India Company. It fixed the Sutlej River as the boundary between the Sikh and British spheres of influence.

treaty-of-amritsar-1846.s: The Treaty of Amritsar of 1846 was an agreement by which the British East India Company sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh, the ruler of Jammu, for 7.5 million rupees. It followed the First Anglo-Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore, which had stripped the Sikh Empire of Kashmir.

treaty-of-apamea.s: The Treaty of Apamea was the peace settlement of 188 BCE between Rome and the Seleucid king Antiochus III after his defeat at the Battle of Magnesia. It stripped the Seleucids of their Anatolian territories beyond the Taurus Mountains, imposed 15,000 talents in war…

treaty-of-fomena.s: The Treaty of Fomena was the peace agreement of 1874 between the British Empire and the Ashanti Empire following the Third Anglo-Ashanti War. The Ashanti agreed to pay a large indemnity in gold, renounce claims to territories in the south and abandon practices the British…

treaty-of-ganja.s: The Treaty of Ganja was an agreement concluded in 1735 between Russia and Iran, then effectively under the control of Nader. Under its terms Russia returned the remaining Caspian territories it had occupied during the collapse of Safavid rule.

treaty-of-jaffa-1192.s: The Treaty of Jaffa of 1192 was the agreement that ended the Third Crusade, concluded between Saladin and Richard I of England. Jerusalem remained under Ayyubid control, while the Crusaders kept a coastal strip from Tyre to Jaffa and Christian pilgrims were allowed to visit…

treaty-of-jaffa-1229.s: The Treaty of Jaffa of 1229 was an agreement between the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil and the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, by which Jerusalem was handed over to Christian control without a battle. Al-Kamil sought Frederick's political support against his own Ayyubid relatives.

treaty-of-kadesh.s: The Treaty of Kadesh, also known as the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, was concluded in 1258 BCE between Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Hattusili III. It followed years of rivalry after the Battle of Kadesh and established peace, mutual defence and the return of…

treaty-of-karlowitz.s: The Treaty of Karlowitz was signed in 1699 between the Ottoman Empire and the Holy League of Austria, Poland-Lithuania, Venice and Russia, ending the war that followed the failed Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683. The Ottomans surrendered Hungary, Transylvania and Podolia.

treaty-of-kucuk-kaynarca.s: The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca was signed in 1774 between the Ottoman Empire and Russia after the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774. It made the Crimean Khanate independent of the Ottomans and gave Russia a foothold on the Black Sea.

treaty-of-lahore.s: The Treaty of Lahore was the peace settlement imposed by the British East India Company on the Sikh Empire after its defeat in the First Anglo-Sikh War of 1845–1846. It stripped the empire of territory, including Kashmir, and limited the size of the Sikh army.

treaty-of-nanjing.s: The Treaty of Nanjing was the peace treaty of 1842 that ended the First Opium War between Britain and Qing China. It ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five ports to British trade and residence, and required China to pay a large indemnity.

treaty-of-nystad.s: The Treaty of Nystad was the peace agreement of 1721 that ended the Great Northern War between Sweden and Russia. Sweden ceded Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and part of Karelia to Russia.

treaty-of-paris-1763.s: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 ended the Seven Years' War between Britain and France and their allies. France ceded Canada and its territory east of the Mississippi to Britain and lost most of its position in India.

treaty-of-peace-1831.s: The Treaty of Peace of 1831 was an agreement between the British and the Ashanti Empire following Ashanti defeat at the Battle of Katamanso in 1826. The Ashanti Empire profile notes that it imposed recognition of the River Pra as the de facto southern boundary of Ashanti…

treaty-of-resht.s: The Treaty of Resht was an agreement of 1732 between Russia and Iran, by which Russia agreed to return parts of the Caspian provinces it had occupied after the collapse of Safavid power. It was negotiated while Nader was restoring Iranian authority.

treaty-of-roskilde.s: The Treaty of Roskilde was a peace treaty concluded in 1658 between Sweden and Denmark-Norway. It followed Charles X Gustav's daring winter march across the frozen straits between the Danish islands.

treaty-of-sevres.s: The Treaty of Sèvres was the peace treaty of 1920 between the Allied powers and the Ottoman Empire after the First World War. It provided for the partition of much of the empire's remaining territory among the Allies and new states.

treaty-of-tordesillas.s: The Treaty of Tordesillas was an agreement of 1494 between Spain and Portugal that divided newly discovered lands outside Europe along a line of longitude west of the Cape Verde Islands. Lands to the west were assigned to Spain and those to the east to Portugal, which later…

treaty-of-utrecht.s: The Treaty of Utrecht was a series of peace agreements of 1713 that ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Philip V was recognised as King of Spain, but Spain lost its European possessions in Italy and the Low Countries, and Britain gained Gibraltar, Minorca and commercial…

treaty-of-verdun.s: The Treaty of Verdun was the agreement of 843 CE that divided the Carolingian Empire among the three surviving grandsons of Charlemagne: Lothar, Louis the German and Charles the Bald. It created West Francia, East Francia and a middle kingdom stretching from the Low Countries…

treaty-of-versailles.s: The Treaty of Versailles was the peace treaty signed in 1919 between the Allied powers and Germany after the First World War. It imposed territorial losses, military restrictions and reparations on Germany, stripped it of its colonies, and included the War Guilt Clause.

treaty-of-zuhab.s: The Treaty of Zuhab was the peace agreement of 1639 between the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire. It ended a long series of wars and left Iraq and Baghdad in Ottoman hands.

trebuchet.s: The trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a pivoting arm to hurl heavy projectiles, either by human traction or by a heavy counterweight. Traction trebuchets were widely used in Chinese warfare, including by the Song Dynasty.

triangular-trade.s: The triangular trade was the Atlantic commercial system linking Europe, West Africa and the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. Manufactured goods went from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans were transported to the Americas, and plantation products such…

tributary-system.s: A tributary system is an arrangement in which subordinate rulers or states acknowledge a superior power by sending regular tribute, often in exchange for recognition, protection or trade access. The best-known example is the Chinese tributary order under the Tang and Ming…

tribute-extraction.s: Tribute extraction is the recurring pattern by which empires drew wealth from conquered or subordinate peoples through regular payments in goods, precious metals, labour or captives, rather than through direct administration. It allowed rapid expansion at low administrative…

tributum.s: Tributum was a direct tax in ancient Rome. Originally a levy on Roman citizens to fund war, it was suspended for citizens in Italy after 167 BCE, and under the empire the term came to denote taxes on provincial land and persons.

trier.s: Trier is a city in western Germany on the Moselle River, founded by the Romans and one of the oldest cities in Germany. In the Holy Roman Empire its archbishop was one of the leading ecclesiastical princes.

triple-entente.s: The Triple Entente was the informal alignment of France, Russia and Britain formed in the years before the First World War. It developed from the Franco-Russian alliance and Britain's agreements with France in 1904 and Russia in 1907.

tripoli.s: Tripoli is a port city on the Mediterranean coast of Libya and historically a major northern terminus of trans-Saharan caravan routes. Goods from the central Sudan, including slaves, leather and ivory, passed through it to Mediterranean markets.

triumph-of-shapur-i.s: The Triumph of Shapur I refers to rock reliefs carved in Iran to commemorate the victories of the Sasanian king Shapur I over Roman emperors in the third century CE. The best known, at Naqsh-e Rostam, shows the captive emperor Valerian kneeling or submitting before the mounted…

trondheim.s: Trondheim is a city in central Norway and the historic centre of the Trøndelag region. Under the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658, Denmark-Norway ceded the province of Trondheim to Sweden, along with Scania and other territories.

trowulan.s: Trowulan is an archaeological site in East Java, Indonesia, identified as the location of the capital of the Majapahit Empire. Its extensive remains include temples, gateways, canals and reservoirs.

truce-of-deulino.s: The Truce of Deulino was an armistice concluded in 1618 between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Muscovy, ending a period of war during Russia's Time of Troubles. It confirmed Polish-Lithuanian possession of Smolensk and Chernigov.

true-cross.s: The True Cross is the name given to relics venerated by Christians as remains of the cross on which Jesus was crucified. A major relic of the cross was carried into battle by the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

tsar.s: Tsar was the title of the supreme ruler of Russia, derived from the Latin Caesar, formally adopted by Ivan IV in 1547. It expressed claims to imperial status and to succession from Byzantium.

tsetse-fly.s: The tsetse fly is a blood-feeding insect of tropical Africa that transmits trypanosomiasis, a disease fatal to horses and cattle. Its presence in forest regions limited the use of cavalry and draught animals.

tuareg.s: The Tuareg are a Berber-speaking, traditionally nomadic people of the central and western Sahara and the Sahel. They controlled important desert routes and oases and at times raided or dominated the cities of the Niger bend.

tuareg-seizure-of-timbuktu.s: The Tuareg seizure of Timbuktu was the capture of the city by Tuareg forces in 1433, as the authority of the Mali Empire over its northern territories weakened. It marked the loss of one of Mali's most important commercial and intellectual centres.

tudhaliya-iv.s: Tudhaliya IV was a king of the Hittite Empire in the thirteenth century BCE, one of its last significant rulers. His reign saw extensive religious reorganisation and building, but also mounting pressures on the empire.

tughlaq-dynasty.s: The Tughlaq dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1320 to the early fifteenth century. Under Muhammad bin Tughlaq the sultanate reached its greatest territorial extent, but his ambitious schemes, such as the transfer of the capital and the token currency, caused serious…

tughril.s: Tughril, or Tughril Beg, was the founder of the Seljuk Empire. Leading Turkic Oghuz forces with his brother Chaghri, he defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and established Seljuk rule in Iran.

tukulti-ninurta-i.s: Tukulti-Ninurta I was a king of Assyria in the thirteenth century BCE, one of the most powerful rulers of the Middle Assyrian period. The Assyrian Empire profile highlights his conquest of Babylon around 1225 BCE and his personal capture of the Kassite king.

tulughma.s: Tulughma was a flanking tactic of Central Asian origin in which mobile cavalry units swept around the enemy's flanks to attack them from the sides and rear. Babur used it at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

tumen.s: A tumen was a military unit of ten thousand soldiers in the Mongol Empire and other steppe armies. It formed the largest division in the decimal system that organised the army into units of ten, one hundred, one thousand and ten thousand.

tunis.s: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia, located near the site of ancient Carthage, and historically an important Mediterranean port. In the medieval and early modern periods it was a northern terminus of trans-Saharan trade.

tunisia.s: Tunisia is a country in North Africa on the Mediterranean, corresponding largely to the ancient region around Carthage. It was the heartland of the Punic Empire, later the Roman province of Africa, and in the medieval period part of the Almohad Caliphate, whose empire…

tunjur.s: The Tunjur were a dynasty that ruled parts of Darfur and Wadai in the eastern Sahel before the seventeenth century. The Wadai Empire profile describes them as a non-Muslim or nominally Muslim ruling group.

tupi.s: Tupi is an indigenous language of Brazil, spoken by the Tupi peoples of the Atlantic coast at the time of Portuguese colonisation. A form of it served as a widely used lingua franca in colonial Brazil, and many Brazilian place names derive from it.

tuqi-king.s: The Tuqi king, or tuqi wang, meaning 'wise king', was one of the highest titles in the Xiongnu Empire. The Xiongnu Empire profile explains that the confederation was divided into left (eastern) and right (western) wings, each administered by a tuqi king who was typically a…

turanshah.s: Turanshah was the last Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, the son of al-Salih Ayyub. He succeeded his father in 1249 during the Seventh Crusade and presided over the defeat of Louis IX.

turkey.s: Turkey is a modern country occupying Anatolia and eastern Thrace. Its territory has been home to many ancient and medieval states, and the Assyrian Empire profile notes the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh in central Anatolia.

turkic-peoples.s: The Turkic peoples are a large family of ethnic groups speaking Turkic languages, originating in the steppes of Inner and Central Asia. The Gokturk Empire was the first state to bear the Turkic name, and Turkic groups later founded or dominated the Seljuk Empire, the Ottoman…

turkification.s: Turkification refers to the process by which regions and populations adopted Turkic language and identity, often following Turkic migration and conquest. The Seljuk Empire profile treats the Seljuk conquests, and especially the opening of Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert…

turkmen.s: The Turkmen, or Turkoman, are Oghuz Turkic peoples historically associated with pastoral nomadism in Central Asia, Iran and Anatolia. Turkmen tribal groups contributed to the forces of many states, including the early Ottoman beyliks, and the Turkmen confederations of the Qara…

turpan-khanate.s: The Turpan Khanate was one of the successor states of the eastern branch of the Chagatai Empire, centred on the oasis of Turpan in what is now Xinjiang. The Chagatai Empire profile notes that the eastern khanate split around 1462 into the Yarkent and Turpan khanates.

tushratta.s: Tushratta was a king of the Mitanni Empire in the fourteenth century BCE. He corresponded with the Egyptian pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten in letters preserved in the Amarna archive and sent his daughter in marriage to Egypt.

twelver-shiism.s: Twelver Shi'ism is the largest branch of Shia Islam, recognising a line of twelve imams, the last of whom is believed to be in occultation. The Ilkhanate profile notes that the Ilkhan Öljeitü's conversion to Twelver Shi'ism briefly promoted it within state structures.

twentieth-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Twentieth Dynasty of Egypt was the last royal dynasty of the New Kingdom, ruling in the twelfth and eleventh centuries BCE. Its early king Ramesses III repelled the Sea Peoples, but later reigns saw economic difficulties, tomb robberies and the growing power of the High…

twenty-fifth-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt was a line of Kushite kings from Nubia who ruled Egypt in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE. Under rulers such as Piye and Taharqa they united the Nile Valley from Napata to the Delta and revived traditional Egyptian religion and art.

twenty-seventh-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Twenty-seventh Dynasty of Egypt is the name given to the first period of Persian rule over Egypt, beginning with Cambyses II's conquest in 525 BCE. Achaemenid kings ruled Egypt as pharaohs through a satrap.

typhus.s: Typhus is a group of bacterial infectious diseases, often spread by lice, that cause fever and can be highly fatal in crowded or wartime conditions. It was among the Eurasian diseases introduced into the Americas after European contact.

tyre.s: Tyre is an ancient Phoenician city on the coast of southern Lebanon, once an island stronghold and a great maritime trading power. Tyrian colonists founded Carthage, the centre of the Punic Empire.

tyrian-purple.s: Tyrian purple is a deep purple dye produced from murex sea snails, named after the Phoenician city of Tyre. Its production required huge numbers of shellfish, making it extremely costly and a symbol of royalty and high status.

teutonic-order.s: The Teutonic Order is a Catholic military order founded at Acre around 1190 during the Third Crusade. From the 1230s it conquered the pagan Prussians and built a state on the Baltic, absorbing the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1237 and taking Pomerelia in 1308.

treaty-of-paris-1259.s: The Treaty of Paris of 1259 was agreed between Louis IX of France and Henry III of England. Henry gave up his claims to Normandy, Anjou, Maine and Poitou, lost under King John, and in return held Gascony as a duchy for which he paid homage to the French king.

treaty-of-paris-1783.s: The Treaty of Paris of 1783 ended the American Revolutionary War. Britain recognised the independence of the United States and accepted borders reaching the Mississippi River in the west, the Great Lakes in the north and Florida in the south.

treaty-of-paris-1814.s: The Treaty of Paris of 1814 made peace between France and the allied powers after Napoleon's first abdication. It restored France roughly to its 1792 borders and returned most of its colonies, but Britain kept Mauritius, the Seychelles, Saint Lucia and Tobago.

treaty-of-paris-1815.s: The Treaty of Paris of November 1815 was signed after Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo and his Hundred Days. It reduced France to its 1790 borders, imposed an indemnity and an allied army of occupation.

treaty-of-paris-1898.s: The Treaty of Paris of December 1898 ended the Spanish–American War. Spain gave up Cuba, which came under American military government, and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, the last for 20 million dollars.

thang-long.s: Thăng Long, 'ascending dragon', was the capital founded by Lý Thái Tổ in 1010 on the Red River, on the site of modern Hanoi. It remained the seat of the Lý, Trần, Lê and Mạc dynasties and of the Trịnh lords for most of the next eight centuries.

treaties-of-nijmegen.s: The Treaties of Nijmegen ended the Franco-Dutch War between France and the Dutch Republic, Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. Spain ceded Franche-Comté and a string of towns in the Spanish Netherlands, including Cambrai, to France.

tupac-inca-yupanqui.s: Túpac Inca Yupanqui was the son of Pachacuti and Sapa Inca from about 1471 to 1493. First as his father's general and then as ruler, he enormously enlarged the Inca Empire, conquering the Chimú kingdom on the north coast, the Cañari and peoples of Ecuador, the Chincha and much…

tian-rong.s: Tian Rong was a member of the royal Tian clan of Qi who led the revived state of Qi after the fall of the Qin. Left out of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, he killed the new kings of Jiaodong and Jibei, drove out the king of Qi and reunited the three…

tay-son-dynasty.s: The Tây Sơn were three brothers from Tây Sơn in central Vietnam who led a peasant rebellion from 1771. They destroyed the Nguyễn lords in the south, defeated a Siamese invasion in 1785, overthrew the Trịnh lords in the north in 1786 and routed a Qing army in 1789 under Nguyễn…

tanganyika-territory.s: Tanganyika Territory was the British-ruled part of former German East Africa, held as a League of Nations mandate from 1922 and a United Nations trust territory from 1946. Britain governed it through indirect rule, keeping local kings and chiefs as native authorities.

takeda-shingen.s: Takeda Shingen was a Japanese daimyo of the Sengoku period who ruled Kai province and expanded into Shinano and Suruga. He fought Uesugi Kenshin in the battles of Kawanakajima and clashed with the Imagawa and Hōjō.

thado-minbya.s: Thado Minbya was the founder of the Ava kingdom in Upper Burma. After Shan raiders sacked Pinya and Sagaing in 1364, he reunited the two courts and in 1365 founded a new capital at Ava, at the meeting of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers.

tipu-sultan.s: Tipu Sultan was ruler of Mysore from 1782, succeeding his father Hyder Ali. Allied with France, he fought the British East India Company in three wars, attacked Travancore in 1789 and lost half his kingdom in 1792.

tomas-cipriano-de-mosquera.s: Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera was a Colombian general who served four times as president. After leading a liberal rebellion in the civil war of 1860–1862, he oversaw the Rionegro constitution of 1863, which created the United States of Colombia as a loose federation.

treaty-of-london-1839.s: The Treaty of London of 1839 was signed by the Netherlands, Belgium and the great powers. It made the Netherlands recognise Belgian independence, nine years after the Belgian Revolution, divided Limburg and Luxembourg between the two countries and guaranteed Belgium's neutrality.

trojan-war.s: The Trojan War was the legendary siege of Troy by the Greeks, told in Homer's Iliad and later poems. Many Greek cities in Anatolia and Cyprus traced their founding to heroes returning from the war.

taejo-of-goryeo.s: Taejo of Goryeo, born Wang Geon, was the founder of the Goryeo dynasty of Korea. A general of Taebong from a trading family of Songak, he was raised to the throne in 918 after the fall of Gung Ye.

turkish-war-of-independence.s: The Turkish War of Independence was fought by the Turkish nationalist movement under Mustafa Kemal against the Allied partition of the Ottoman Empire. The Ankara government defeated Armenian forces in the east, French forces in the south and Greek armies in western Anatolia.

thomas-maitland.s: Sir Thomas Maitland was a British general and colonial governor who served as governor of Ceylon from 1805 to 1811 and of Malta from 1813. From 1815 he was also the first Lord High Commissioner of the United States of the Ionian Islands, where his autocratic manner earned him…

tailapa-ii.s: Tailapa II was a feudatory of the Rashtrakuta dynasty who claimed descent from the Chalukyas of Badami. In 973 he overthrew the last Rashtrakuta king, Karka II, and founded the Western Chalukya Empire in the Deccan.

tarquinius-superbus.s: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Tarquin the Proud, was by tradition the seventh and last king of Rome. Roman historians portrayed him as a tyrant who extended Rome's power over Latium, allied with Tusculum through marriage and built the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol.

tekle-haymanot-saint.s: Tekle Haymanot was an Ethiopian monk and saint, one of the most revered figures of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Saints' lives describe him preaching in the pagan kingdom of Damot and founding the monastery of Debre Libanos in Shewa, which became the leading monastic house of…

tekle-haymanot-of-gojjam.s: Tekle Haymanot, earlier known as Ras Adal, was ruler of Gojjam in north-western Ethiopia. Emperor Yohannes IV crowned him negus of Gojjam and Kaffa in 1881, but he was defeated by Menelik of Shewa at Embabo in 1882.

thanh-hoa.s: Thanh Hoa is a region of north-central Vietnam south of the Red River delta. It was the home country of the Ho dynasty, which built the stone citadel of Tay Do there, and of Le Loi, who led the war against Ming rule from Lam Son in 1418.

thubten-gyatso.s: Thubten Gyatso was the 13th Dalai Lama. He fled the British invasion of Lhasa in 1904 and a Qing army in 1910, but returned after the Qing collapse and in 1913 proclaimed Tibet's independence.

three-bishoprics.s: The Three Bishoprics were the cities and ecclesiastical principalities of Metz, Toul and Verdun in Lorraine. Henry II of France occupied them in 1552 in alliance with German Protestant princes, and the Peace of Westphalia formally ceded them to France in 1648.

tian-shi-king-of-qi.s: Tian Shi was a member of the royal Tian family of Qi who became king of Qi during the rising against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu moved him to the minor kingdom of Jiaodong on the Shandong peninsula.

tiberius-sempronius-gracchus-consul-177-.s: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was a Roman general and statesman, father of the reformers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. As governor of Hispania Citerior from 180 to 178 BCE he ended the First Celtiberian War with treaties that kept peace in central Spain for a generation, and…

tippu-tip.s: Tippu Tip was a Swahili-Arab trader from Zanzibar who built a commercial empire in the eastern Congo basin, dealing in ivory and slaves. From his base at Kasongo he ruled much of Manyema in the 1870s and 1880s.

treaty-of-campo-formio.s: The Treaty of Campo Formio, signed in October 1797, ended the war between Austria and the French Republic after Napoleon's Italian campaign. Austria ceded the Austrian Netherlands and recognised French aims on the left bank of the Rhine, while receiving Venice, whose republic…

treaty-of-turkmenchay.s: The Treaty of Turkmenchay, signed in February 1828, ended the Russo-Persian War of 1826 to 1828. Qajar Iran ceded the khanates of Erivan and Nakhichevan to Russia, confirmed earlier losses such as Talysh, paid a large indemnity and granted Russian subjects legal privileges.

tunku-abdul-rahman.s: Tunku Abdul Rahman was a prince of the Kedah royal family who led the United Malays National Organisation from 1951. He negotiated Malaya's independence from Britain, proclaiming it in 1957, and became the first prime minister of the Federation of Malaya.

turgut-reis.s: Turgut Reis, known in Europe as Dragut, was an Ottoman corsair and admiral. A lieutenant of Hayreddin Barbarossa, he raided the coasts of Italy and Spain, helped take Tripoli from the Knights Hospitaller in 1551 and became its governor, and defeated a Spanish fleet at Djerba…

the-tale-of-igors-campaign.s: The Tale of Igor's Campaign is an anonymous Old East Slavic epic poem, usually dated to the late 12th century. It tells of the failed raid of Prince Igor Sviatoslavich of Novgorod-Seversky against the Cumans in 1185 and calls on the Rus' princes to unite.

tai-lu-people.s: The Tai Lü are a Tai-speaking people of the upper Mekong, living chiefly in Sipsong Panna (Xishuangbanna) in southern Yunnan and in neighbouring parts of Laos, Myanmar and Thailand. Theravada Buddhist rice farmers, they formed the kingdom centred on Chiang Hung, which paid…

tang-jingsong.s: Tang Jingsong was a Qing official from Guangxi who was governor of Taiwan when the Treaty of Shimonoseki ceded the island to Japan in 1895. Local gentry made him president of the short-lived Republic of Formosa, proclaimed on 25 May 1895 in the hope of foreign intervention.

tardu-shad.s: Tardu Shad was a son of Tong Yabghu Qaghan of the Western Turkic Khaganate, installed around 625 as yabghu, or viceroy, of Tokharistan, the former Hephthalite lands of Bactria, with his seat at Kunduz. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited his court around 630, shortly before…

tauke-khan.s: Tauke Khan was khan of the Kazakh Khanate in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, the last to hold the three juz together. He is remembered for the law code Zhety Zhargy, the 'Seven Charters', which regulated custom, feuds and property among the Kazakh tribes, and for his…

tayang-khan.s: Tayang Khan was ruler of the Naiman, a powerful confederation of the western Mongolian steppe, after the death of his father Inanch Bilge Khan in the 1190s split the realm between him and his brother Buyruk. In 1204 he marched against Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, and was…

tell-al-rimah.s: Tell al-Rimah is an archaeological mound in northern Iraq, west of Mosul, usually identified with ancient Karana or Qattara. Excavated by David Oates between 1964 and 1971, it revealed a temple and palace of the early second millennium BCE with an archive of letters of Queen…

teutoburg-forest.s: The Teutoburg Forest is a range of low wooded hills in northern Germany, running about 100 km south-east from the Osnabrück area to near Paderborn. It gave its name to the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, in which Arminius destroyed three Roman legions.

theodoric-the-great.s: Theodoric the Great was king of the Ostrogoths who invaded Italy at the request of Emperor Zeno, defeated Odoacer and ruled the peninsula from Ravenna from 493 to 526. He kept Roman law, the senate and the civil administration while his Goths formed the army, and built a…

third-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Third Dynasty of Egypt ruled from about 2686 to 2613 BCE and opened the Old Kingdom. Its best-known king, Djoser, was buried in the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by his official Imhotep and the first monumental stone building in Egypt.

thomas-buchanan-governor.s: Thomas Buchanan was an American colonisation agent who became governor of Bassa Cove in 1836 and in 1839 the first governor of the Commonwealth of Liberia, which united Monrovia, Bassa Cove and other settlements. A cousin of the future US president James Buchanan, he organised…

thomas-palaiologos.s: Thomas Palaiologos was a Byzantine prince, youngest brother of Constantine XI, and despot of the Morea from 1428. He completed the conquest of the Latin Principality of Achaea in 1430–1432 and ruled the Peloponnese jointly with his brother Demetrios.

tian-an.s: Tian An was a grandson of King Jian, the last king of the State of Qi, who fought in the rebellion against the Qin dynasty and followed Xiang Yu to Julu. In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE he was made King of Jibei, north of the Ji River, but within months Tian Rong, excluded…

tian-du.s: Tian Du was a general of Qi who joined Xiang Yu's campaign against the Qin dynasty and in 206 BCE was made King of Qi, with his capital at Linzi, when Xiang Yu divided the old State of Qi into three kingdoms. Tian Rong, the clan strongman left out of the settlement, drove him…

tian-guang.s: Tian Guang was the son of Tian Rong and king of Qi during the Chu–Han Contention. After his father was killed resisting Xiang Yu in 205 BCE, his uncle Tian Heng rallied Qi and installed him as king, with himself as chancellor.

tian-shan.s: The Tian Shan, the 'Heavenly Mountains', is a great mountain system of Central Asia stretching about 2,500 km from Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan east into Xinjiang. Its northern and southern foothills held chains of oases and pastures used by the Silk Road and by nomadic powers…

toirdelbach-ua-conchobair.s: Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair was King of Connacht from 1106 to 1156 and one of the strongest high kings of Ireland. He built bridges and castles across the Shannon, used fleets on rivers and lakes, and in 1118 divided Munster into Desmond and Thomond by the Treaty of Glanmire.

toqtoa-beki.s: Toqto'a Beki was chief of the Uduyit Merkit and the most powerful leader of the Merkit confederation of the forest and steppe south of Lake Baikal in the late 12th century. A long-standing enemy of Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, whose wife Börte the Merkit had abducted, he…

traprain-law.s: Traprain Law is a hill in East Lothian, Scotland, crowned by one of the largest hillforts in Britain. A centre of the Votadini from the Iron Age through the Roman period, it received Roman goods in quantity, and in 1919 excavators found the Traprain Law Treasure, a hoard of…

treaty-of-amiens.s: The Treaty of Amiens, signed in March 1802 between France and Britain, with Spain and the Batavian Republic, briefly ended the French Revolutionary Wars. Britain returned most of its conquests but kept Trinidad, taken from Spain, and the former Dutch possessions on Ceylon.

treaty-of-bongaya.s: The Treaty of Bongaya was signed in November 1667 between Sultan Hasanuddin of Gowa and the Dutch East India Company, whose commander Cornelis Speelman, allied with Arung Palakka of Bone, had defeated Makassar. Gowa had to expel other Europeans, give the Company a trade…

treaty-of-breda-1667.s: The Treaty of Breda, signed in July 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War between England and the Dutch Republic, with France and Denmark. Each side kept what it held: England kept New Netherland, renamed New York, while the Dutch kept Suriname and the nutmeg island of Run.

treaty-of-brest-litovsk.s: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918 between Soviet Russia and the Central Powers, took Russia out of the First World War. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine, and ceded Kars, Ardahan and Batum to the Ottoman Empire, which pushed the…

treaty-of-bromsebro-1645.s: The Treaty of Brömsebro, signed in August 1645, ended the Torstenson War between Denmark-Norway and Sweden. Denmark ceded the Baltic islands of Gotland and Ösel and the Norwegian provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen, exempted Sweden from the Sound tolls and pledged Halland for…

treaty-of-lausanne.s: The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, settled the conflict between the Allies and the Turkish nationalist government, replacing the Treaty of Sèvres. It recognised Turkey's borders in Anatolia and eastern Thrace, including Smyrna, confirmed Greek sovereignty over…

treaty-of-madrid-1670.s: The Treaty of Madrid of 1670 was concluded between England and Spain to settle their conflicts in the Caribbean. Spain recognised English possession of Jamaica, taken in 1655, together with the Cayman Islands and the other territories England then held in the Americas, while…

treaty-of-madrid-1750.s: The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 between Portugal and Spain replaced the line of the Treaty of Tordesillas with borders in South America based on actual occupation. Portugal secured most of the Amazon basin and the interior of Brazil, giving up Colonia do Sacramento in exchange…

treaty-of-stensby.s: The Treaty of Stensby was concluded in 1238 at Stensby in Zealand between King Valdemar II of Denmark and the Livonian Order, mediated by the papal legate William of Modena. It returned northern Estonia, with Rävala, Harjumaa and Virumaa, to Denmark, while Järvamaa stayed with…

treaty-of-vereeniging.s: The Treaty of Vereeniging, signed in Pretoria on 31 May 1902, ended the Second Boer War. The South African Republic and the Orange Free State accepted British sovereignty as the Transvaal Colony and the Orange River Colony, in exchange for promised self-government,…

trinh-kiem.s: Trinh Kiem was a Vietnamese general and founder of the power of the Trinh lords. Son-in-law of the Le loyalist leader Nguyen Kim, he took command of the Later Le restoration forces after Nguyen Kim's death in 1545 and fought the Mac dynasty from Thanh Hoa, becoming the real…

trinh-tung.s: Trinh Tung was the Trinh lord who ruled northern Vietnam behind the Later Le emperors from 1570 to 1623. A son of Trinh Kiem, he captured Thang Long from the Mac dynasty in 1592 and executed the Mac emperor Mac Mau Hop, restoring the Le court to the capital.

tughlugh-timur.s: Tughlugh Timur was khan of Moghulistan, the eastern part of the Chagatai Khanate, from 1347 to 1363. Raised to the throne by the Dughlat amir Puladchi, he converted to Islam around 1354, reportedly with many of his followers.

tukoji-rao-i-puar.s: Tukoji Rao I Puar was a Maratha commander who, with his brother Jivaji Rao, accompanied the Peshwa Baji Rao I into Malwa and received Dewas around 1728. The brothers' joint holding developed into two princely states sharing one capital and dividing land and revenues: Dewas…

tyrrhenian-sea.s: The Tyrrhenian Sea is the part of the Mediterranean bounded by mainland Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, named from the Greek word for the Etruscans. In antiquity it carried Etruscan, Greek and Carthaginian trade, and Greek colonies on the Ionian coast of southern Italy,…

temple-of-athena-alea.s: The Temple of Athena Alea at Tegea in Arcadia was the centre of a regional cult of Athena by the 8th century BCE. After a fire in 395 BCE it was rebuilt in the 4th century BCE to designs by the sculptor Scopas, and was considered one of the finest temples of the Peloponnese.

tvrtko-i-of-bosnia.s: Tvrtko I of Bosnia, of the Kotromanić dynasty, ruled Bosnia as ban from 1353 and in 1377 was crowned king at Mile, claiming the Serbian crown through descent from the Nemanjić dynasty. He extended his rule over western Serbia, Zachlumia and much of the Dalmatian coast, making…

tarentum.s: Tarentum, Greek Taras, was a Spartan colony founded around 706 BCE on the Gulf of Taranto in southern Italy, on the site of modern Taranto. With a fine harbour and rich trade, it became the leading Greek city of the region, heading the Italiote League from the fourth century BCE.

thebes-greece.s: Thebes was the leading city of Boeotia in central Greece and the dominant member of the Boeotian League. It sided with Persia during the invasion of 480–479 BCE, but under Epaminondas and Pelopidas it defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE and briefly became the strongest power…

tu-duc.s: Tự Đức was emperor of Vietnam under the Nguyen dynasty from 1847 to 1883, its longest-reigning ruler. A scholarly Confucian, he persecuted Catholics and resisted reform.

the-pale.s: The Pale was the area around Dublin under direct English rule in late medieval Ireland, covering parts of Dublin, Meath, Louth and Kildare. By the 15th century English authority had shrunk to this fortified district, defended by ditches and castles against Gaelic lords who…

tomas-estrada-palma.s: Tomás Estrada Palma was a veteran of the Cuban independence struggle who became the first President of Cuba in 1902, when the United States military government withdrew. His government left a treasury surplus, but his disputed re-election in 1906 provoked a Liberal revolt.

taejo-of-joseon.s: Taejo of Joseon, born Yi Seong-gye, was a Goryeo general who won fame fighting Japanese pirates and Red Turban invaders. Ordered to attack Ming China in 1388, he turned his army back at Wihwa Island and took control of the government.

temple-of-hera-lacinia.s: The Temple of Hera Lacinia was a Doric temple on the headland of Capo Colonna near Croton in southern Italy. Its sanctuary was one of the most important in Magna Graecia and served as the common religious centre of the Italiote League.

thibaw-min.s: Thibaw Min was the last king of the Konbaung dynasty of Burma, reigning from 1878 to 1885. His reign began with the killing of many royal relatives and faced revolts among the Shan states, including the Limbin Confederacy.

tropaeum-alpium.s: The Tropaeum Alpium, or Trophy of Augustus, is a Roman victory monument built in 7 to 6 BCE at La Turbie, above Monaco, on the road through the Maritime Alps. It celebrated Augustus's conquest of the Alpine peoples, and its inscription, recorded by Pliny the Elder, lists 45…

thomas-cochrane-10th-earl-of-dundonald.s: Thomas Cochrane, Lord Cochrane and later 10th Earl of Dundonald, was a British naval officer who commanded the navies of independence movements in South America. In 1820 he carried José de San Martín's Liberating Expedition from Chile to Peru, and as admiral of the Brazilian…

treaty-of-hue-1884.s: The Treaty of Huế of 6 June 1884, negotiated by the French diplomat Jules Patenôtre, confirmed French protection over Vietnam after the conquest of Tonkin. It replaced the harsher Harmand Treaty of 1883, leaving Annam under the Nguyễn emperor with French oversight and placing…

tamar-of-georgia.s: Tamar was queen regnant of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, and her reign marks the height of the medieval Georgian kingdom. Her second husband, David Soslan, was an Alanian prince.

trenggana.s: Trenggana was sultan of Demak in Java from about 1521 to 1546, under whom the sultanate reached its greatest extent, conquering much of eastern Java and taking Sunda Kelapa. He was killed during a campaign against Panarukan in 1546, and the succession war that followed broke…

taceddin-bey.s: Taceddin Bey was a Turkmen chief who founded the Taceddinid beylik around Niksar in the Pontic hinterland of northern Anatolia in the mid-14th century, as Ilkhanid authority faded. He married Eudokia, daughter of the Trebizond emperor Alexios III, linking his house with its…

tadhg-mor-ua-cellaig.s: Tadhg Mór Ua Cellaig (died 1014) was king of Uí Maine, the kingdom of the Uí Chellaig (O'Kellys) in east Connacht. He fought for Brian Boru at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014 and was killed there, one of the leading men recorded in the Irish annals as falling on Brian's side.

tadhg-ocarroll-baron-of-ely.s: Tadhg O'Carroll was chief of the O'Carrolls of Éile in the Irish midlands in the mid-16th century. Under the Tudor policy of surrender and regrant he gave up his lands to the crown in 1552 and received them back with the title Baron of Ely.

tafari-benti.s: Tafari Benti (1921–1977) was an Ethiopian army general who became chairman of the Derg, the military council that overthrew Haile Selassie, and thus head of state in November 1974. Largely a figurehead, he was killed in a shoot-out at a Derg meeting in February 1977, after…

tahir-ibn-husayn.s: Tahir ibn Husayn (775–822) was a Persian general who won the civil war for the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, defeating the armies of al-Amin and taking Baghdad in 813. Made governor of Khurasan in 821, he omitted the caliph's name from the Friday prayer shortly before his death.
