tai-mao.s: The Tai Mao are a Tai-speaking people of the Shweli river valley on today's China–Myanmar border, part of the wider Shan peoples. Their kingdom of Mong Mao was a regional power in the 14th century until Ming armies broke it in the 1440s, and several northern Shan states, such…

taifa-of-beja-and-evora.s: The Taifa of Beja and Évora was a short-lived Muslim principality in the south of present-day Portugal, ruled by Sidray ibn Wazir in the 1140s when Almoravid rule in al-Andalus broke down. His family, the Banu Wazir, also took Badajoz in 1145, and he moved between alliance and…

taj-al-din-al-hasani.s: Taj al-Din al-Hasani (1885–1943) was a Syrian religious scholar and politician, son of a leading Damascus cleric. He headed the government of the State of Syria under the French mandate in 1928–1931 and 1934–1936, and in 1941 the Free French made him president of Syria, an…

taj-al-din-harb.s: Taj al-Din Harb ibn Muhammad was the Nasrid malik of Sistan who ruled for nearly fifty years until his death in 1215. Ruling from Zaranj, he kept his house in power by accepting the overlordship first of the Seljuks and then of the Ghurids, whose campaigns he supported with…

taj-al-muluk-buri.s: Taj al-Muluk Buri (died 1132) was the Burid ruler of Damascus from 1128, succeeding his father Toghtekin, founder of the dynasty. In 1129 he suppressed the Ismaili Assassins in the city and repelled a crusader attack on Damascus.

taj-chan-ahk.s: Taj Chan Ahk (741–c. 795) was the most powerful king of the Maya city of Cancuén in Guatemala, reigning from 757.

takeda-nobutora.s: Takeda Nobutora (1494–1574) was a Japanese warlord who unified Kai province under the Takeda clan and built its residence at Tsutsujigasaki in Kōfu. In 1541 he was deposed by his son Takeda Shingen and sent into exile in Suruga, the domain of the Imagawa.

takelot-iii.s: Takelot III was an Egyptian pharaoh of the 8th century BCE, a son of Osorkon III, who first served as High Priest of Amun at Thebes and then as co-ruler with his father. He belonged to the line of kings based at Thebes and Herakleopolis often called the Twenty-third Dynasty,…

tamim-ibn-buluggin.s: Tamim ibn Buluggin was a Zirid prince who ruled the Taifa of Málaga from about 1073 to 1090, while his brother Abd Allah ruled Granada. The brothers quarrelled over territory, and both were deposed by the Almoravid ruler Yusuf ibn Tashfin in 1090 and sent into exile in North…

tan-date.s: Tan Date was the leader under whom Abron (Bono) migrants moved west in the late 17th century, escaping the rising power of the Ashanti Empire, and settled around Bondoukou on the border of present-day Ghana and Ivory Coast. Abron tradition remembers him as the founder and…

tancredo-neves.s: Tancredo Neves (1910–1985) was a Brazilian politician from Minas Gerais who served as prime minister in 1961–1962. In January 1985 an electoral college chose him as the first civilian president after two decades of military rule, but he fell ill on the eve of his inauguration…

tangaxuan-ii.s: Tangaxuan II (died 1530) was the last independent cazonci, or ruler, of the Purépecha Empire in western Mexico. After the fall of Tenochtitlan he submitted peacefully to the Spanish under Cristóbal de Olid in 1522, but he was later arrested by Nuño de Guzmán, tortured to…

tanjung-pura.s: Tanjung Pura is a town on the Batang Serangan River in Langkat, North Sumatra, Indonesia, that served as the royal seat of the Langkat Sultanate. Its Azizi Grand Mosque, built around 1900 with income from tobacco plantations and oil, is the sultanate's best-known monument.

tapa-chermoev.s: Tapa Chermoev (1882–1937) was a Chechen landowner, oil industrialist and former officer of the Russian imperial guard. In 1917–1918 he led the Union of the Peoples of the North Caucasus and became the first head of government of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus.

taqi-al-din-umar.s: Taqi al-Din Umar (died 1191) was a nephew of Saladin and one of his leading commanders. He held Hama from 1178 and Mayyafariqin and other lands in the Jazira from 1185, and his mamluk Qaraqush led troops west into Tripolitania.

tarcondimotus-ii-philopator.s: Tarcondimotus II Philopator was king of the Tarcondimotid realm in eastern Cilicia in the late 1st century BCE and early 1st century CE. Son of Tarcondimotus I, who died fighting for Mark Antony in 31 BCE, he was deprived of his kingdom by Octavian but restored by Augustus in…

tarnovo-constitution.s: The Tarnovo Constitution was the first constitution of the Principality of Bulgaria, adopted by a constituent assembly at Veliko Tarnovo on 16 April 1879. One of the most liberal of its time, it set up a single-chamber National Assembly, guaranteed civil rights and limited the…

tashkent-soviet.s: The Tashkent Soviet was the council of workers' and soldiers' deputies in Tashkent, dominated by Russian railway workers and soldiers, which seized power in Russian Turkestan in November 1917. It excluded the Muslim majority from government and in February 1918 sent troops…

tasker-h-bliss.s: Tasker H. Bliss (1853–1930) was a United States Army general who governed the Moro Province in the southern Philippines from 1906 to 1909.

tattooed-serpent.s: Tattooed Serpent (died 1725) was the war chief of the Natchez in present-day Mississippi and brother of the Great Sun, their paramount ruler. He generally kept peace with the French colony of Louisiana, and his funeral in 1725, at which wives and retainers were put to death to…

te-agbanlin.s: Te Agbanlin was the founder of the kingdom of Porto-Novo, known locally as Hogbonou, in present-day Benin. According to tradition he was a prince of Allada who left after a succession dispute in the late 17th century and settled by the coastal lagoon among Yoruba-speaking…

teanum-sidicinum.s: Teanum Sidicinum, modern Teano in northern Campania, Italy, was the chief town of the Oscan-speaking Sidicini, set in the hills between the Roccamonfina volcano and the Volturno. Their conflict with the Samnites in 343 BCE drew Rome into its first war with Samnium.

tegin-shah.s: Tegin Shah was a ruler of the Turk Shahi dynasty of Kabul and Gandhara in the early 8th century. He received titles from the Tang emperor of China in the 720s and, according to Chinese records, abdicated in 739 in favour of his son Fromo Kesaro.

teimuraz-ii-of-kakheti.s: Teimuraz II (1700–1762) was a Georgian king of the Bagrationi dynasty who ruled Kakheti and, with the approval of Nader Shah of Persia, Kartli from 1744. He passed Kakheti to his son Erekle II, and the two worked together to defend eastern Georgia.

tej-narsingh-malla.s: Tej Narsingh Malla was the last Malla king of Lalitpur (Patan) in the Kathmandu valley, raised to the throne by its nobles in the 1760s as Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha closed in on the valley. When Gorkha forces took Lalitpur in 1768 he fled to Bhaktapur, and he was captured…

tel-dan-stele.s: The Tel Dan stele is a fragmentary Aramaic inscription of the 9th century BCE found in 1993–1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel. Probably set up by Hazael of Aram-Damascus, it boasts of victories over a king of Israel and a king of the 'House of David', the earliest widely…

tell-afis.s: Tell Afis is an archaeological site in north-western Syria, south-west of Aleppo, identified with ancient Hazrek (Hatarikka), capital of the Aramean kingdom of Luash. An Aramaic stele found there records how Zakkur, king of Hamath and Luash, withstood a siege of Hazrek by a…

tell-tayinat.s: Tell Tayinat is an archaeological site in the Amuq plain of Hatay, south-eastern Turkey, identified with Kunulua, capital of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Patina (Unqi). Excavations have uncovered palaces, temples, Luwian inscriptions and a copy of the succession treaty of the…

tem-baiteke.s: Tem Baiteke was a high chief of Abemama in the central Gilbert Islands, in present-day Kiribati, in the mid-19th century. Using firearms obtained from European traders, he brought the neighbouring atolls of Aranuka and Kuria under his rule, creating a small island kingdom.

ten-years-war-1118-1127.s: The Ten Years' War of 1118–1127 was a conflict between the Italian communes of Milan and Como, sparked by a dispute over the bishopric of Como and control of trade on Lake Como. Milan, supported by allied towns, besieged Como and destroyed it in 1127.

ten-years-war.s: The Ten Years' War of 1868–1878 was the first major Cuban war of independence against Spain. It began when Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his enslaved workers and proclaimed independence at La Demajagua on 10 October 1868, and was fought by the Republic of Cuba in Arms mainly…

teodoro-de-croix.s: Teodoro de Croix (1730–1792) was a Flemish-born officer in Spanish service who became the first commandant general of the Internal Provinces of northern New Spain in 1776. He reorganised the frontier presidios and the defence against Apache and Comanche raids.

teofilo-braga.s: Teófilo Braga (1843–1924) was a Portuguese writer, literary historian and positivist thinker who led the provisional government of the First Portuguese Republic after the revolution of 5 October 1910. He served again briefly as president in 1915, after the resignation of…

teriimaevarua-iii.s: Teriimaevarua III (1871–1932) was the last queen of Bora Bora in the Society Islands, succeeding as a child in 1873 and reigning until France annexed the island, a process completed in 1895. Her reign saw growing French influence across the Leeward Islands after the annexation…

teriitaria-ii.s: Teriitaria II (c. 1790–1858) was queen of Huahine in the Society Islands from 1815 and a wife of King Pōmare II of Tahiti.

terrance-drew.s: Terrance Drew (born 1976) is a Kittitian physician and politician who has been Prime Minister of Saint Kitts and Nevis since August 2022. Leader of the Saint Kitts and Nevis Labour Party, he took office after his party won the general election that month, ending the Team Unity…

tetrapolitan-confession.s: The Tetrapolitan Confession was a Protestant statement of faith presented at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 by four south German imperial cities: Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau. Drafted mainly by Martin Bucer and Wolfgang Capito, it stood between Lutheran and…

thado-minsaw-of-prome.s: Thado Minsaw was a son of King Narapati of Ava and governor of Prome who rebelled in 1482 during a succession crisis and made Prome an independent kingdom. He ruled it for several decades, holding the lower Irrawaddy between Ava and the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy.

thamal-al-dulafi.s: Thamal al-Dulafi was a commander and governor of Tarsus in the early 10th century who led land and naval raids from the Abbasid frontier into Byzantine Anatolia and the Aegean. He was among the leading figures of the thughur, the Muslim frontier zone in Cilicia, and took part…

thefarie-velianas.s: Thefarie Velianas was a ruler of the Etruscan city of Caere around 500 BCE. He is named in the Pyrgi Tablets, gold sheets with Etruscan and Phoenician texts found at Caere's port of Pyrgi in 1964, which record his dedication of a sanctuary to the goddess Uni, equated with the…

themistokli-germenji.s: Themistokli Gërmenji (1871–1917) was an Albanian nationalist from Korçë who led guerrilla bands against Ottoman and Greek forces. In 1916 he became prefect of the Autonomous Albanian Republic of Korçë, set up under French military protection during the First World War.

theobald-i-of-blois.s: Theobald I of Blois (died 975), known as the Trickster, was a vassal of Hugh the Great who by about 940 held the counties of Blois, Chartres and Tours. He married Luitgard, daughter of Herbert II of Vermandois, and founded the house of Blois, whose counts rivalled the early…

theodore-ii-muzaka.s: Theodore II Muzaka (died 1389) was an Albanian lord of the Muzaka family who held Berat and the surrounding region of central Albania in the late 14th century. According to tradition he died fighting the Ottomans in the Serbian-led coalition at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389.

theodore-rshtuni.s: Theodore Rshtuni (died 655) was an Armenian prince and military commander who led the defence of Armenia against the first Arab raids. In 653 he made a treaty with Muawiya, then governor of Syria, accepting Arab overlordship in return for autonomy and the right to keep…

theodoros-negris.s: Theodoros Negris (1790–1824) was a Greek scholar and diplomat from Constantinople who served the Ottoman administration before joining the Greek War of Independence. In 1821 he drew up the Legal Order of Eastern Continental Greece and led its regional government, the…

theoktistos-bryennios.s: Theoktistos Bryennios was a Byzantine general and strategos of the theme of the Peloponnese in the 840s. Sent by the regency of Empress Theodora, he subdued the Slavic peoples of the region, including the Melingoi and Ezeritai of the Taygetus mountains, who kept their own…

theophilus-eaton.s: Theophilus Eaton (1590–1658) was a London merchant who in 1638 founded the New Haven Colony in present-day Connecticut with the Puritan minister John Davenport. He served as its governor from 1639 until his death, ruling a strict Puritan settlement in which only church members…

theophilus-shepstone.s: Sir Theophilus Shepstone (1817–1893) was a British colonial official in South Africa who, as Natal's chief official for African affairs from 1845 to 1875, created a system of indirect rule through chiefs on reserved locations. In 1877 he annexed the South African Republic…

theron-of-acragas.s: Theron of Acragas (died 472 BCE) was tyrant of the Greek city of Acragas in Sicily from about 488 BCE. He expelled Terillus from Himera around 483 BCE, provoking a Carthaginian invasion, and with his son-in-law Gelon of Syracuse destroyed Hamilcar's army at the Battle of…

thietmar-of-merseburg.s: Thietmar of Merseburg (975–1018) was a Saxon noble who became bishop of Merseburg in 1009. His Latin Chronicon, covering the Ottonian kings and emperors up to 1018, is a principal source for eastern Saxony, the Slavs beyond the Elbe, Poland and Kievan Rus.

thihathu.s: Thihathu (died 1325) was the youngest of three Shan-Burmese brothers who repelled the Mongols and took power in central Burma after the fall of Pagan. In 1313 he founded a new capital at Pinya and proclaimed himself heir to the Pagan kings.

third-anglo-burmese-war.s: The Third Anglo-Burmese War was a short campaign in November 1885 in which British forces advanced up the Irrawaddy and took Mandalay, deposing King Thibaw, the last king of the Konbaung dynasty. Upper Burma was annexed on 1 January 1886, completing British rule over the whole…

third-carlist-war.s: The Third Carlist War of 1872–1876 was a civil war in Spain in which supporters of the pretender Carlos VII tried to win the throne. The Carlists built a state with its own administration in Navarre, the Basque provinces and parts of Catalonia, fighting the governments of…

third-mithridatic-war.s: The Third Mithridatic War of 73–63 BCE was the last war between Rome and Mithridates VI of Pontus. It began when Mithridates invaded Bithynia, which its last king Nicomedes IV had bequeathed to Rome.

third-sacred-war.s: The Third Sacred War of 356–346 BCE was fought between the Phocians, who seized the sanctuary of Delphi, and the Delphic Amphictyony led by Thebes, the Thessalians and the Locrians. The Phocians paid mercenaries with the temple treasures.

thohanbwa.s: Thohanbwa (died 1543) was a Shan prince, son of Sawlon of Mohnyin, who became king of Ava after the Shan confederation captured the city in 1527. Distrusting the Burmese monkhood, he became notorious for killing monks and plundering pagodas.

thomas-carleton.s: Thomas Carleton (c. 1735–1817) was an Irish-born British army officer who became the first governor of New Brunswick when it was separated from Nova Scotia in 1784 to receive Loyalist refugees.

thomas-chittenden.s: Thomas Chittenden (1730–1797) was a farmer and political leader who served as governor of the Vermont Republic from 1778 to 1789 and again from 1790, and as the first governor of the state of Vermont after it joined the United States in 1791. During the Revolutionary War he…

thomas-gorges.s: Thomas Gorges (1618–1670) was an English lawyer and a cousin of Sir Ferdinando Gorges, proprietor of the Province of Maine. He served as deputy governor of the province from 1640 to 1643, holding courts and organising government in Ferdinando's absence, and was mayor of the…

thomas-hutchinson-governor.s: Thomas Hutchinson (1711–1780) was a Boston merchant, historian and politician who served as lieutenant governor and then governor of the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1771 to 1774. A loyalist, he enforced British policy, and his insistence that the taxed tea be landed led…

thomas-langley.s: Thomas Langley (c. 1363–1437) was an English churchman and royal servant who was Bishop of Durham from 1406 to 1437 and twice Lord Chancellor, under Henry IV and Henry V.

thomas-munro.s: Sir Thomas Munro (1761–1827) was a Scottish soldier and administrator of the East India Company. He developed the ryotwari system, under which land revenue was settled directly with individual cultivators, and applied it as Governor of the Madras Presidency from 1820 until his…

thomas-muntzer.s: Thomas Müntzer (c. 1489–1525) was a radical German preacher of the Reformation who broke with Martin Luther and preached that the godly must bring in God's kingdom by force.

thomas-picton.s: Sir Thomas Picton (1758–1815) was a Welsh-born British general who governed Trinidad after its capture from Spain in 1797. His harsh rule, including the authorised torture of a young girl, Luisa Calderón, led to his trial in London.

thomas-preston-1st-viscount-tara.s: Thomas Preston (1585–1655) was an Irish Catholic soldier who served Spain in the Netherlands before returning in 1642 to command the army of Leinster for Confederate Ireland. He was defeated by Michael Jones at Dungan's Hill in 1647, held Waterford against Cromwell's forces in…

thomas-warner.s: Sir Thomas Warner (c. 1580–1649) was an English captain who founded the first English colony in the Caribbean on Saint Christopher (St Kitts) in 1624.

thomas-robert-bugeaud.s: Thomas-Robert Bugeaud (1784–1849) was a French marshal who, as governor-general of Algeria from 1840 to 1847, led the conquest of the country against Abd al-Qadir. He used mobile columns and a scorched-earth policy of raids, defeated the Moroccan army at Isly in 1844 and…

thorgeir-ljosvetningagodi.s: Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði was a pagan chieftain and the lawspeaker of the Icelandic Althing from 985 to 1001. At the Althing of 999 or 1000, chosen to settle the dispute between pagans and Christians, he lay under a cloak for a day and then ruled that all Icelanders should…

three-collas.s: The Three Collas, Colla Uais, Colla Fo Chrí and Colla Menn, were legendary brothers descended in Irish tradition from Conn of the Hundred Battles. In the 4th or 5th century they are said to have destroyed Emain Macha, the royal centre of the Ulaid, and won lands in mid-Ulster.

three-gorges.s: The Three Gorges are the narrow, steep-sided canyons of the Yangtze River between Fengjie in Chongqing and Yichang in Hubei: the Qutang, Wu and Xiling gorges. For centuries they were the main route between Sichuan and the middle Yangtze, and controlled access to the lands of…

three-qins.s: The Three Qins were the kingdoms of Yong, Sai and Di created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE in Guanzhong, the old heartland of Qin, for the surrendered Qin generals Zhang Han, Sima Xin and Dong Yi. Intended to block Liu Bang in Hanzhong, they were conquered by him within months,…

thuringian-forest.s: The Thuringian Forest is a wooded mountain range in central Germany, running about 150 kilometres from the Werra valley south-east towards the Thuringian Highlands; its highest peak, the Großer Beerberg, reaches 983 metres. In the Middle Ages and early modern period its slopes…

thuringian-highlands.s: The Thuringian Highlands are an upland region of slate hills in south-eastern Thuringia, Germany, linking the Thuringian Forest with the Franconian Forest. Poor in farmland but rich in timber and slate, the area was divided among small lordships, notably the many lines of the…

thuwayni-ibn-abdullah.s: Thuwayni ibn Abdullah (died 1797) was a sheikh of the Al Saadun, the ruling family of the Muntafiq tribal confederation of southern Iraq. He seized Basra from the Ottoman authorities in 1787 but was driven out by forces sent from Baghdad.

tian-heng.s: Tian Heng (died 202 BCE) was a member of the royal house of the old state of Qi who, after the fall of Qin, made himself and his relatives kings of Qi and fought both Xiang Yu and Liu Bang. After Han Xin conquered Qi he fled to an island with some 500 followers.

tiburcio-carias-andino.s: Tiburcio Carías Andino (1876–1969) was a Honduran general and leader of the National Party who was president from 1933 to 1949. He extended his term through constitutional changes, ruled as a dictator with the backing of the United States fruit companies and suppressed…

tieba-traore.s: Tieba Traoré (died 1893) was king of Kénédougou in present-day Mali and Burkina Faso, who turned the loose chiefdom into a strong state and moved its capital to Sikasso, which he fortified with great earthen walls. He withstood a long siege by Samori Ture in 1887–1888 and…

tigernan-ua-ruairc.s: Tigernán Ua Ruairc (died 1172) was king of Breifne for nearly fifty years and one of the most powerful Irish rulers of the 12th century. The abduction of his wife Derbforgaill by Diarmait Mac Murchada in 1152 fed a long feud, and he helped drive Diarmait into exile in 1166,…

tir-eoghain.s: Tír Eoghain, 'Eogan's land', was the Gaelic kingdom of the O'Neills in mid-Ulster, the core of modern County Tyrone. Its kings descended from the Cenél nEógain branch of the northern Uí Néill and became the most powerful Gaelic rulers in late medieval Ireland.

tiridates-iii-of-armenia.s: Tiridates III was Arsacid king of Armenia from the late 3rd century until about 330, restored with Roman support after a period of Sasanian rule. Converted by Gregory the Illuminator, he made Christianity the state religion of Armenia in about 301, traditionally the first…

tirot-sing.s: Tirot Sing (1802–1835) was a Khasi chief of Nongkhlaw in the hills of present-day Meghalaya, India. When the British began building a road through his territory to link the Brahmaputra and Surma valleys, he led an uprising in 1829 that grew into a four-year war.

tirumala-nayak.s: Tirumala Nayak (died 1659) was the most famous ruler of the Madurai Nayak dynasty in southern India, reigning from 1623 to 1659. He threw off the authority of the declining Vijayanagara rulers, fought Mysore and Bijapur, and built the Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal palace in…

tisquesusa.s: Tisquesusa (died 1537) was the last independent zipa of Bacatá, the southern Muisca realm on the high plain of present-day Bogotá in Colombia. When the Spanish under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada arrived in 1537 he avoided battle and withdrew, and he was killed by a Spanish…

tito-venier.s: Tito Venier was a Venetian noble of Crete who in 1363 led the revolt of the island's Venetian colonists against Venice, sparked by a new tax for the harbour of Candia. The rebels proclaimed the Republic of Saint Titus, named after the island's patron saint, and sought Greek…

titu-cusi-yupanqui.s: Titu Cusi Yupanqui (1529–1571) was ruler of the Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba from 1563, a son of Manco Inca. He negotiated with the Spanish, admitted Augustinian missionaries and dictated an account of the conquest from the Inca point of view.

todo-takatora.s: Tōdō Takatora (1556–1630) was a Japanese warlord who served several masters, including Toyotomi Hideyoshi, before siding with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara in 1600. Renowned as a castle builder, he worked on Edo, Osaka and Nijō castles.

toghan-arslan.s: Toghan Arslan, nicknamed the Hunchback, was the best-documented ruler of the Dilmaçoğulları, a Turkmen dynasty that held Bitlis and Erzen south-west of Lake Van. In the early 12th century he allied with the Artuqid Ilghazi against the Georgians and the Crusaders, and fought…

tokhtamysh.s: Tokhtamysh (died 1406) was a Mongol khan descended from Jochi who, with the support of Timur, became khan of the White Horde and by 1380 reunited it with the Golden Horde. He sacked Moscow in 1382, restoring Mongol overlordship over the Russian principalities, but then turned…

tokugawa-mitsukuni.s: Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1701) was the second lord of the Mito domain and a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu. He began the compilation of the Dai Nihonshi, a vast history of Japan, which fostered the Mito school of learning with its emphasis on loyalty to the emperor.

tokugawa-muneharu.s: Tokugawa Muneharu (1696–1764) was the seventh lord of the Owari domain from 1730. In open defiance of the austerity reforms of the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune, he encouraged spending, theatre and pleasure quarters in Nagoya, which made the city flourish.

tokugawa-nariaki.s: Tokugawa Nariaki (1800–1860) was the ninth lord of the Mito domain from 1829 and a leading advocate of coastal defence and the expulsion of foreigners. He founded the Kōdōkan school and promoted the Mito school's loyalty to the emperor.

tokugawa-yorifusa.s: Tokugawa Yorifusa (1603–1661) was the eleventh son of Tokugawa Ieyasu and the founder of the Mito branch of the Tokugawa family, one of the three senior houses (gosanke) entitled to provide a shogun. He received the Mito domain in Hitachi province in 1609 and ruled it until…

tokugawa-yorinobu.s: Tokugawa Yorinobu (1602–1671) was the tenth son of Tokugawa Ieyasu and the founder of the Kii branch of the Tokugawa family, one of the three senior houses (gosanke). Moved to Wakayama in 1619, he ruled the Kii domain and built up its castle town.

tokugawa-yoshikatsu.s: Tokugawa Yoshikatsu (1824–1883) was lord of the Owari domain from 1849. Punished in the Ansei purge for opposing Ii Naosuke, he later commanded the shogunate's first expedition against Chōshū in 1864.

tokugawa-yoshimune.s: Tokugawa Yoshimune (1684–1751) was lord of the Kii domain from 1705 and became the eighth Tokugawa shogun in 1716, the first from a branch line. His Kyōhō reforms cut spending, raised rice revenue, introduced a petition box and relaxed the ban on Western books.

tokugawa-yoshinao.s: Tokugawa Yoshinao (1601–1650) was the ninth son of Tokugawa Ieyasu and the founder of the Owari branch of the Tokugawa family, the highest-ranking of the three senior houses (gosanke). He ruled the Owari domain from Nagoya Castle, built for him from 1610, and promoted…

tole-bi.s: Tole Bi (1663–1756) was a judge and leader of the Senior Juz of the Kazakhs, remembered for his wisdom and eloquence. With Kazybek Bi of the Middle Juz and Ayteke Bi of the Junior Juz he is traditionally credited with helping to draw up the law code of Tauke Khan, the Zheti…

tom-adams.s: Tom Adams (1931–1985) was a Barbadian politician who was prime minister from 1976 until his death in office in 1985. The son of Grantley Adams, the island's first premier, he led the Barbados Labour Party and backed the United States-led intervention in Grenada in 1983.

tom-blount.s: Tom Blount (died 1739) was a chief of the northern Tuscarora towns in North Carolina in the early 18th century. Unlike Hancock's southern towns, his people stayed out of the Tuscarora War of 1711–1715 and made a separate peace with the colony, which recognised him as leader of…

tomas-garrigue-masaryk.s: Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk (1850–1937) was a Czech philosopher and politician who led the campaign abroad for Czechoslovak independence during the First World War. He became the first president of Czechoslovakia in 1918 and was re-elected three times before retiring in 1935,…

tomasi-kulimoetoke-ii.s: Tomasi Kulimoetoke II (1918–2007) was the Lavelua, or king, of Uvea (Wallis) in Wallis and Futuna from 1959 until his death. His reign of nearly fifty years spanned the islands' change from French protectorate to overseas territory in 1961.

tomasz-dabal.s: Tomasz Dąbal (1890–1937) was a Polish lawyer and peasant activist who in November 1918 led, with the priest Eugeniusz Okoń, the short-lived Republic of Tarnobrzeg, which demanded land reform. He later became a communist deputy, moved to the Soviet Union and was executed there…

tomyris.s: Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic Iranian people east of the Caspian Sea, in the 6th century BCE. According to Herodotus, after Cyrus the Great of Persia captured her son by a trick, she defeated the Persian army in 530 BCE, killed Cyrus and had his head put in…

tran-thai-tong.s: Trần Thái Tông (1218–1277), born Trần Cảnh, was the first emperor of the Trần dynasty of Đại Việt. Married as a child to the young empress Lý Chiêu Hoàng in 1225, he received the throne when she abdicated, ending the Lý dynasty, while his uncle Trần Thủ Độ held real power.

tran-nhan-tong.s: Trần Nhân Tông (1258–1308) was emperor of Đại Việt from 1278 to 1293. With the general Trần Hưng Đạo he defeated the Mongol Yuan invasions of 1285 and 1287–1288.

tran-trong-kim.s: Trần Trọng Kim (1883–1953) was a Vietnamese scholar and historian, author of a widely read outline history of Vietnam, who served as prime minister of the Japanese-backed Empire of Vietnam from April to August 1945. His government ended when Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated during…

transcaucasian-sejm.s: The Transcaucasian Sejm was the legislature of Transcaucasia that met in Tiflis from February to May 1918, formed from Georgian, Armenian and Azerbaijani deputies elected to the Russian Constituent Assembly. Under Ottoman military pressure after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, it…

treaty-of-ankara-1921.s: The Treaty of Ankara (1921) was the agreement signed on 20 October 1921 between France and the Turkish nationalist government of the Grand National Assembly, negotiated by Henry Franklin-Bouillon. France ended its war in Cilicia, withdrew its troops and in practice recognised…

treaty-of-bardo.s: The Treaty of Bardo was signed on 12 May 1881 at the Ksar Saïd palace near Tunis by Muhammad as-Sadiq Bey, under pressure from an invading French army. It placed the Beylik of Tunis under French protection, giving France control of its foreign affairs and defence while the bey…

treaty-of-cordoba.s: The Treaty of Córdoba was signed on 24 August 1821 at Córdoba, Veracruz, by Agustín de Iturbide and Juan O'Donojú, the last Spanish head of government of New Spain. It accepted the Plan of Iguala, recognising Mexico as an independent constitutional monarchy, and opened the way…

treaty-of-fez.s: The Treaty of Fez was signed on 30 March 1912 by Sultan Abd al-Hafid of Morocco and France after the Agadir Crisis. It made Morocco a French protectorate, with a resident-general holding real power while the sultan and his makhzen government were kept in place.

treaty-of-fontainebleau-1762.s: The Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762) was a secret agreement of 3 November 1762 in which France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi, together with New Orleans, to its ally Spain. Made as the Seven Years' War was ending, it compensated Spain for losing Florida to Britain and…

treaty-of-fontainebleau-1807.s: The Treaty of Fontainebleau (1807) was a secret agreement of 27 October 1807 between Napoleonic France and Spain to invade and partition Portugal. It allowed French troops to cross Spain and promised the Bourbon rulers of Etruria a new realm in northern Portugal in exchange…

treaty-of-glanmire.s: The Treaty of Glanmire was an agreement of 1118 by which Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, king of Connacht and claimant to the high kingship of Ireland, partitioned the Kingdom of Munster. Desmond in the south went to the MacCarthys and Thomond in the north to the O'Briens.

treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo.s: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848, ended the Mexican–American War. Mexico recognised the Rio Grande as the border of Texas and ceded Alta California and New Mexico, about half of its territory, to the United States in return for 15 million dollars and…

treaty-of-gulistan.s: The Treaty of Gulistan was signed in October 1813 between the Russian Empire and Qajar Iran, ending the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813. Persia recognised Russian possession of Dagestan, eastern Georgia and most of the khanates of the eastern Caucasus, including Talysh, and…

treaty-of-hamburg-1701.s: The Treaty of Hamburg (1701) settled the succession dispute that followed the extinction of the Güstrow line of the House of Mecklenburg in 1695. Signed on 8 March 1701 under imperial mediation, it divided Mecklenburg between Duke Frederick William, who received…

treaty-of-luneville.s: The Treaty of Lunéville was signed on 9 February 1801 between the French Republic and Emperor Francis II after Austrian defeats at Marengo and Hohenlinden. It confirmed the terms of Campo Formio, ceding the whole left bank of the Rhine to France and recognising French…

treaty-of-mandsaur.s: The Treaty of Mandsaur was signed on 6 January 1818 between the British East India Company and the Holkar state of Indore, after its defeat at Mahidpur in the Third Anglo-Maratha War. Indore ceded territory, accepted a British resident and a subsidiary force, and became a…

treaty-of-montgomery.s: The Treaty of Montgomery was agreed on 29 September 1267 between Henry III of England and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, brokered by the papal legate Ottobuono. Henry recognised Llywelyn as Prince of Wales, with overlordship over the other Welsh lords, in return for homage and a large…

treaty-of-pilar.s: The Treaty of Pilar was signed on 23 February 1820 by the governor of Buenos Aires, Manuel de Sarratea, and the federalist caudillos Francisco Ramírez of Entre Ríos and Estanislao López of Santa Fe, after their victory at Cepeda. It ended the central Directorate, accepted a…

treaty-of-ribe.s: The Treaty of Ribe, issued on 5 March 1460, was the charter by which the estates of Schleswig and Holstein elected King Christian I of Denmark as duke of Schleswig and count of Holstein after the Schauenburg line of Holstein-Rendsburg died out. In return he promised that the…

treaty-of-rome.s: The Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957 by Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, founded the European Economic Community. It created a customs union and common market, with a commission, council, assembly and court, and took effect on 1…

treaty-of-ryswick.s: The Treaty of Ryswick, signed in September and October 1697 at Rijswijk near The Hague, ended the Nine Years' War between Louis XIV's France and the Grand Alliance. France returned most of its gains since 1679 but kept Strasbourg, and recognised William III as king of England.

treaty-of-simulambuco.s: The Treaty of Simulambuco was signed on 1 February 1885 between Portugal and the princes and chiefs of Cabinda, on the Atlantic coast north of the Congo River. It placed the area, once ruled by the kingdoms of Ngoyo and Kakongo, under Portuguese protection, securing Portugal's…

treaty-of-stadtilm.s: The Treaty of Stadtilm of 1599 divided the lands of the counts of Schwarzburg in Thuringia between the brothers of the late Count Günther XLI. It created the lines of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt and Schwarzburg-Sondershausen, each holding parts of the Upper and Lower Lordships.

treaty-of-taif.s: The Treaty of Ta'if was signed on 20 May 1934 between Saudi Arabia and the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen after the brief Saudi–Yemeni War. Yemen recognised Saudi rule over Asir, Jizan and Najran, and the two kingdoms agreed to peace, friendship and the return of each other's…

treaty-of-the-hague-1661.s: The Treaty of The Hague (1661) was signed on 6 August 1661 between the Dutch Republic and Portugal. The Dutch recognised Portuguese sovereignty over Brazil, which they had lost with the surrender of Recife in 1654, in return for an indemnity of four million cruzados, paid…

treaty-of-the-hague-1720.s: The Treaty of The Hague (1720) was signed on 17 February 1720, ending the War of the Quadruple Alliance. Philip V of Spain gave up his conquests in Italy, and Victor Amadeus II of Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia with Emperor Charles VI.

treaties-of-tilsit.s: The Treaties of Tilsit were signed in July 1807 by Napoleon with Alexander I of Russia and Frederick William III of Prussia, after the French victory at Friedland. Prussia lost about half its territory: its Polish lands formed the Duchy of Warsaw, and Danzig became a free city…

treaty-of-tolentino.s: The Treaty of Tolentino was signed on 19 February 1797 between Pope Pius VI and the French Republic, represented by Napoleon Bonaparte. The Papal States gave up Avignon and the Comtat Venaissin, ceded the Legations of Bologna, Ferrara and Romagna, left Ancona under French…

treaty-of-torrellas.s: The Treaty of Torrellas was an arbitration of 8 August 1304, led by King Denis of Portugal, that settled the war between Castile and Aragon over the Kingdom of Murcia. Aragon kept the northern part of Murcia, including Alicante, Elche and Orihuela, while Castile kept the rest.

treaty-of-waitangi.s: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed on 6 February 1840 at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands by William Hobson for the British Crown and more than 40 Māori chiefs, later joined by about 500 more. Its English and Māori texts differ on sovereignty and governorship, a source of lasting…

treaty-of-windsor-1175.s: The Treaty of Windsor (1175) was agreed between Henry II of England and Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last High King of Ireland, after the Anglo-Norman invasion. Ruaidrí accepted Henry as overlord and paid tribute, keeping Connacht and authority over Irish kings outside the…

treaty-of-xanten.s: The Treaty of Xanten was signed on 12 November 1614 to settle the War of the Jülich Succession, which followed the death of the last duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg in 1609. It divided the inheritance between the two main claimants: the Elector of Brandenburg received Cleves, Mark…

treaty-of-yandabo.s: The Treaty of Yandabo was signed on 24 February 1826 by the British East India Company and the Konbaung kingdom of Burma, ending the First Anglo-Burmese War. Burma gave up its claims to Assam, Manipur, Cachar and Jaintia, ceded Arakan and Tenasserim to the British, paid an…

tribal-hidage.s: The Tribal Hidage is an Anglo-Saxon list of 35 peoples south of the Humber, giving the number of hides, units of land assessment, attributed to each. It probably records tribute owed to a Mercian or possibly Northumbrian overlord and is usually dated between the 7th and 9th…

trisong-detsen.s: Trisong Detsen was emperor of Tibet from 755 to about 797, the second of the three great 'religious kings' of the Tibetan Empire. His armies briefly took the Tang capital Chang'an in 763 and extended Tibetan power along the Silk Road.

tran-quy-khoang.s: Trần Quý Khoáng, known by his reign name Trùng Quang, was the second and last emperor of the Later Trần dynasty, which resisted the Ming occupation of Vietnam. He was proclaimed in 1409 by followers of the generals Đặng Tất and Nguyễn Cảnh Chân, whom the first Later Trần…

tsugaru-nobumasa.s: Tsugaru Nobumasa was the fourth daimyo of the Hirosaki Domain in northern Honshu, ruling from 1656 until his death in 1710. A student of Confucian and military learning under Yamaga Sokō, he reformed the domain's administration and finances, opened new rice fields, promoted…

tuanku-abdul-rahman.s: Tuanku Abdul Rahman was the Yang di-Pertuan Besar, or ruler, of Negeri Sembilan from 1933 and the first Yang di-Pertuan Agong, the elected supreme head of state, of the Federation of Malaya. Chosen by the Conference of Rulers, he took office at independence in 1957 and served…

tuanku-gocah-pahlawan.s: Tuanku Gocah Pahlawan was the founder of the ruling house of Deli in north-eastern Sumatra. According to Deli tradition he was a commander in the service of Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh, who sent him in the 1630s to secure the east coast of Sumatra for Aceh.

tuanku-umar-johan-alamsyah.s: Tuanku Umar Johan Alamsyah was the founder of the Serdang Sultanate in north-eastern Sumatra. A son of Tuanku Panglima Paderap of Deli, he was passed over in the succession dispute that followed his father's death around 1723 and, with the support of local chiefs, set up a…

tufa-wugu.s: Tufa Wugu was the founder of Southern Liang, one of the Sixteen Kingdoms of northern China. Chief of the Tufa branch of the Xianbei, settled in the Huangshui valley of eastern Qinghai, he broke away from Later Liang in 397 and proclaimed himself king.

tughril-iii.s: Tughril III was the last Seljuk sultan of Iraq and western Iran, reigning from 1176 to 1194. For most of his reign real power lay with the Eldiguzid atabegs of Azerbaijan, who had placed him on the throne.

tughtakin-ibn-ayyub.s: Tughtakin ibn Ayyub, titled Sayf al-Islam, was a brother of Saladin who ruled Ayyubid Yemen from 1182 until his death in 1197. Sent to restore order after the conquest by his brother Turanshah, he took Sanaa and other highland strongholds from local rulers and built up Ta'izz…

tughtekin.s: Tughtekin was a Turkish commander who became atabeg, or guardian, of the Seljuk prince Duqaq of Damascus and, after Duqaq's death in 1104, the effective ruler of the city. He founded the Burid dynasty, named after his son Taj al-Muluk Buri.

tui-kanokupolu.s: Tuʻi Kanokupolu is the title of the third and youngest of Tonga's royal lines, founded in the early 17th century by a son of the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua. Its holders became the effective rulers of Tonga, while the Tuʻi Tonga kept a sacred status.

tui-viti.s: Tui Viti, meaning 'king of Fiji', is the title claimed in the mid-19th century by Seru Epenisa Cakobau, the paramount chief of Bau. Accepted by some foreign consuls but disputed by rivals such as the Tongan chief Enele Maʻafu, the claim was realised in the Kingdom of Fiji…

tukoji-rao-holkar-iii.s: Tukoji Rao Holkar III was the Maharaja of Indore from 1903 to 1926. Taking full powers in 1911, he presided over the growth of Indore's cotton trade and public works.

tun-abdul-majid.s: Tun Abdul Majid was the Bendahara, or chief minister, of the Johor-Riau sultanate who became the first of the hereditary Bendahara rulers of Pahang. Around 1770 the sultan granted him Pahang as a fief, and his descendants governed it from Pekan as Raja Bendahara.

tuoba-shiyijian.s: Tuoba Shiyijian was prince of Dai, the Tuoba Xianbei state in modern Inner Mongolia, from 338 to 376. Having spent years as a hostage at the Later Zhao court, he introduced officials, written laws and a more settled capital at Shengle.

tupac-amaru.s: Túpac Amaru was the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State of Vilcabamba, ruling from 1571 to 1572. He succeeded his brother Titu Cusi Yupanqui and broke off negotiations with the Spanish.

tupua-tamasese-lealofi-iii.s: Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III was a Samoan paramount chief and leader of the Mau, the non-violent movement for self-government against New Zealand rule. Imprisoned in New Zealand in 1928 for resisting taxes, he returned to Samoa in 1929.

turar-ryskulov.s: Turar Ryskulov was a Kazakh revolutionary and Soviet statesman. As a leading Muslim communist he headed the government bodies of the Turkestan ASSR in the early 1920s and proposed a Turkic Soviet republic, which Moscow rejected as nationalist.

turdakun-usubaliyev.s: Turdakun Usubaliyev was First Secretary of the Communist Party of Kirghizia, and so leader of the Kirghiz SSR, from 1961 to 1985, the longest tenure of any Soviet Kyrgyz leader. His rule brought industrial growth and the expansion of Frunze, now Bishkek, but also patronage…

turin-king-list.s: The Turin King List, or Turin Royal Canon, is an Egyptian papyrus written in hieratic in the reign of Ramesses II and now in the Museo Egizio in Turin. It lists gods and kings of Egypt with their reign lengths, including many minor rulers of the Second Intermediate Period…

turki-ibn-abdullah.s: Turki ibn Abdullah was the founder of the second Saudi state, the Emirate of Nejd. A grandson of Muhammad ibn Saud, he survived the Ottoman-Egyptian destruction of Diriyah in 1818 and in 1824 drove the Egyptian garrison from Riyadh, which he made his capital.

turku-castle.s: Turku Castle is a medieval fortress at the mouth of the Aura River in Turku, south-western Finland, begun around 1280 as a Swedish stronghold. For centuries it was the main seat of royal power in Finland.

tuscarora-war.s: The Tuscarora War was fought in North Carolina from 1711 to 1715 between the Tuscarora and their allies and British colonists. Angered by land seizures, trading abuses and the enslavement of their people, the southern Tuscarora attacked settlements along the Neuse and Pamlico…

tuxtla-mountains.s: The Tuxtla Mountains, or Sierra de los Tuxtlas, are a volcanic range on the Gulf of Mexico coast in southern Veracruz, Mexico. Their basalt was quarried by the Olmecs and hauled to San Lorenzo and other centres to carve colossal heads, table-thrones and other monuments.

twelve-articles.s: The Twelve Articles were the demands of the peasants of Upper Swabia, drawn up at Memmingen in March 1525 during the German Peasants' War. Written by the furrier Sebastian Lotzer with the preacher Christoph Schappeler, they asked for the right to choose pastors, the abolition…

tzanetos-grigorakis.s: Tzanetos Grigorakis, known as Zanetbey, was bey of the Mani in the southern Peloponnese from 1782 to 1798, under Ottoman overlordship. From the Grigorakis clan of the Gytheio area, he governed the feuding Maniot chieftain families and paid the tribute owed to the Ottomans.
